Merged from A (dsp:vedic-rites-as-final-goal-bhagavad-gita) and B (same id as here).

question: Is the Bhāgavata's final purport non-dual knowledge or devotion?

sides.position: Non-dual knowledge: the Bhāgavata's mark is the oneness of Brahman and self, its sole aim kaivalya (12.13.12); forms are superimposed (1.3.30-33); Śuka's last word is 'I am Brahman' (12.5.11); devotion purifies for knowledge.

Devotion: bhakti is the supreme dharma (1.2.6); devotees refuse the five liberations, even oneness, without service (3.29.13) and desire not even freedom from rebirth (11.14.14); only bhakti wins the Lord (11.14.20); Kṛṣṇa is Bhagavān himself.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: each school reads the other's key verses as subordinate; P1 (level) and P4 (stage) are candidate principles but both traditions reject them.
candidate_readings: P1-level: the devotional passages speak at the conventional level, the non-dual ones at the ultimate (the Advaita reading; rejected by Vaiṣṇavas).
P4-stage: knowledge is a stage within devotion, or devotion within knowledge (each school's own subordination).
The text's own synthesis: BhP 1.2.11 names one non-dual reality as Brahman, Paramātman and Bhagavān, and 11.2.42 has devotion, experience and detachment arise together.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Gauḍīya, Mādhva and Vallabha authors deny that devotion is a means to be transcended; Advaitins deny that personal distinction survives liberation.

checks.note: All cited verses located (BhP 1.2.6, 1.2.11, 1.3.28, 1.3.30-33, 2.9.32-35, 3.29.13, 11.2.42, 11.14.14, 11.14.20, 12.5.11, 12.13.12). The school positions are summarized at the level of each school's known stance, not checked against the commentaries.

question: Is devotion or knowledge the higher and more direct means, and is oneness with the Lord to be desired?

sides.position: Devotion alone wins the Lord; motiveless devotion is greater than liberation; pure devotees refuse even oneness without service.
arguments: neither yoga nor Sāṃkhya nor austerity win me as does devotion (11.14.20)
devotion dissolves the subtle body (3.25.33)
devotees do not accept ekatva (3.29.13)

sides.position: Knowledge of the non-dual Self liberates; even the practice of samādhi is bondage from the absolute standpoint; the jñānī is dearest to the Lord.
arguments: resting in awareness one is free now (Aṣṭāvakra 1.4)
the knower is dearest (Uddhava Gītā 11.19.3)
knowledge alone removes ignorance (Rāma Gītā 7.5.9)

sides.position: Devotion is the lamp without which knowledge does not shine; from devotion knowledge, realization, dispassion and liberation follow quickly.
arguments: as eyes see nothing at night without a lamp (AR 3.4.46-47)

reconciliation.explanation: The Uddhava Gītā itself assigns knowledge, action and devotion to different dispositions (11.20.6-8), and the Devī Gītā grades devotion upward into non-dual knowledge.
reconciliation.detail: Under P3 the paths suit different temperaments; under P4 devotion is a means that matures into knowledge (Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa, Devī Gītā). The Kapila Gītā's refusal of oneness is not reconciled by this reading.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Gauḍīya and other Vaiṣṇava readers reject the reading of bhakti as a mere means to non-dual knowledge; Advaita readers reject the claim that devotion is higher than liberation.

candidate_readings: by temperament (P3)
by stage, devotion maturing into knowledge (P4)
devotion as the end in itself (Vaiṣṇava)
knowledge as the end (Advaita)

queries: local texts at the refs cited by dsp:bhakti-jnana-precedence
checks.note: All cited verses verified: BhP 11.14.20-21, 3.25.33 (vulgate), 3.29.13, 11.19.3 ('jñānī priyatamo 'to me'); AG 1.4, 1.15; AR 7.5.9, 3.4.45-47 (the lamp), 1.1.51; DBhP 7.37.26-27.

question: Is ignorance (avidyā) a positive entity (bhāva-rūpa) that is the material cause of the world-appearance, or is it superimposition/non-apprehension itself?

sides.position: Positive: ignorance is a beginningless, indescribable, positive power, proved by perception ('I am ignorant'), inference and presumption; Padmapāda calls it an insentient power.
arguments: Mere absence cannot be a material cause.
The report 'I knew nothing' after sleep shows positive experience of ignorance.

sides.position: Maṇḍana: ignorance is non-apprehension and misapprehension residing in the jīvas. Swami Satchidanandendra (recent): for Śaṅkara avidyā is superimposition itself (BSBh intro), not a positive root-ignorance; the later doctrine departs from Śaṅkara.
arguments: Śaṅkara defines avidyā as adhyāsa.
A positive ignorance would itself need explaining.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the question concerns what Śaṅkara taught and whether a positive ignorance is required; the prakriyā principle is invoked by traditionalists but rejected by the modern critic.
candidate_readings: P1-level/P6-upaya: both are empirical-level explanations of the one error (traditional compendia).
Historical reading: Śaṅkara's usage is phenomenological (adhyāsa), the Vivaraṇa's is causal-explanatory; they answer different questions.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Satchidanandendra holds the mūlāvidyā doctrine to be an error, not a method; Vivaraṇa scholars hold the positive ignorance necessary to explain the world's material cause.

question: Are the vīra and divya dispositions (and the five tattvas) permitted in the Kali age?

sides.position: (Kālīvilāsa) No: the divya and vīra dispositions 'do not exist, do not exist' in the Kali age; all classes worship in the paśu disposition (4.2-3); divya belonged to Satya–Tretā, vīra to Tretā–Dvāpara (6.10-16).

(Mahānirvāṇa) Yes, with restrictions: the five tattvas are proper to Śakti worship (5.22-24), the tantric path is the only one for this age (2.7-15), but in the Kali age the last tattva is only with one's own wife and householders use the sweet triad (6.14; 8.170-171).
(Kulārṇava) The Kaula is highest without any age restriction, though only for the tested and eligible (2.7-8; 2.30-36).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the Kālīvilāsa denies outright what the Mahānirvāṇa and Kulārṇava allow under conditions.
candidate_readings: P4-stage: the Mahānirvāṇa's substitutes for householders show a graded permission; the Kālīvilāsa's rule may address ordinary worshippers of the four classes.
P2-standpoint: the Kālīvilāsa speaks from the standpoint of the age (cosmic), the Kulārṇava from that of the qualified individual.
Not reconcilable if the Kālīvilāsa's 'does not exist' is taken as a universal prohibition.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Each text presents its own rule as Śiva's command for the Kali age.

question: On what terms were women ordained, and can the Theravāda bhikkhunī order be restored?

sides.position: The canonical account: the Buddha, after three refusals, granted Mahāpajāpatī's going forth on condition of the eight principles of respect, affirming that women can realise all four fruits, and predicted a shorter duration of the true Dhamma; at the First Council Ānanda was charged with having urged it. (Traditionalist position, recent:) the Theravāda bhikkhunī lineage lapsed and cannot be revived, since ordination requires an existing bhikkhunī Saṅgha of the same lineage.
arguments: The requirement of dual ordination (garudhamma 6).

sides.position: (Revivalist position, recent:) the order can be restored with the help of bhikkhunīs of a lineage held to descend from Saṅghamittā (the Dharmaguptaka lineage of East Asia), or by monks alone under the Buddha's allowance for monks to ordain nuns; the canon affirms women's capacity for arahantship and records a flourishing Bhikkhunī Saṅgha (Thig).
arguments: Cv 10.1.3 and the Therīgāthā.
Revival ordinations held from 1996 (Sarnath) and 1998 (Bodh Gayā) onward (recent).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: a living Vinaya question within Theravāda.
candidate_readings: P4-stage: the garudhammas as contextual rules of the founding situation (revivalist reading)
Strict Vinaya reading: the procedural requirements are not open to reinterpretation (traditionalist reading)
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The traditionalist side rejects any reading that treats the Vinaya's procedural rules as provisional.

notes: Canonical content recorded faithfully; the modern debate is flagged recent. See U38's dsp:bhiksuni-ordination-revival for the Tibetan (Mūlasarvāstivāda) debate and U50's dsp:women-caste-liberation.

question: Can the full ordination of nuns be introduced in the Mūlasarvāstivāda (Tibetan) tradition?

sides.position: Only by a procedure valid under the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya, which requires a quorum of bhikṣuṇīs of the same lineage; such a lineage is absent in Tibet (conservative view).
The Dharmaguptaka bhikṣuṇī lineage, living in East Asia, can supply the nuns' side of a dual ordination (reformist view).

historical_debates.name: International Congress on Buddhist Women's Role in the Saṅgha
historical_debates.accounts: Congress proceedings
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: No consensus reached

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: whether and how full ordination of nuns can be conferred where the Mūlasarvāstivāda bhikṣuṇī lineage was never transmitted.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Many Tibetan Vinaya authorities hold that mixing Vinaya lineages or ordination by monks alone is not valid under the Mūlasarvāstivāda code.

candidate_readings: Vinaya reading: dual ordination with Dharmaguptaka bhikṣuṇīs and Mūlasarvāstivāda bhikṣus.
Vinaya reading: ordination by bhikṣus alone, as permitted at the order's beginning.

question: How should Digambara image worship be performed, and are the bhaṭṭārakas authorities?

sides.position: Worship with fresh flowers, fruits, lamps and sweets, seated; the bhaṭṭārakas are legitimate heads; the attendant deities (Padmāvatī, Kṣetrapāla) may be honoured.
arguments: Long temple custom
The bhaṭṭārakas preserved the tradition when naked monks were few

sides.position: Offer only non-living substances (rice, dry fruits), standing; reject the bhaṭṭārakas; worship of attendant deities is wrong faith.
arguments: Non-harm in worship
Ṭoḍarmal's critique of wrong faith and clerical laxity

reconciliation.explanation: Both worship the same Jina images and accept Kundakunda; the manner of offering is a difference of ritual path.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Terāpantha holds worship of attendant deities to be wrong faith, a point no reconciliation of method covers.

question: Does liberation contain bliss (and consciousness)?

sides.position: Mainstream Nyāya: liberation is absolute release from pain; there is no proof of an eternal pleasure manifested in it, and one who strives for liberation out of attachment to pleasure is not freed; the liberated self has neither pleasure nor cognition. Pleasure bound up with pain is to be relinquished like food mixed with honey and poison.
arguments: NBh 1.1.22 against 'some' who hold eternal pleasure is manifested in liberation.
Fear of a liberation 'without pleasure and without consciousness' is listed among forms of false knowledge (NBh 1.1.2).
Navya-Nyāya: liberation is a destruction of pain not contemporaneous with any prior absence of pain (Muktivāda).

sides.position: Liberation is the absence of contact with a body and of new appearance when adṛṣṭa is exhausted; a quiescence like fire whose fuel is burnt (no special qualities of the self remain).
arguments: VS 5.2.20 (Candrānanda); Praśastapāda.

sides.position: Bhāsarvajña (a minority within Nyāya): liberation is the absolute cessation of pain qualified by the experience of eternal pleasure.
arguments: Nyāyasāra and Nyāyabhūṣaṇa.

sides.position: Liberation is the realization of the self as Brahman, being-consciousness-bliss; a liberation without consciousness or bliss would be no better than a stone's state — a charge pressed against Nyāya (e.g. in Śrīharṣa's Naiṣadhīyacarita, as usually cited).
arguments: Polemical verse on Gautama and 'stone-hood' (ref from memory).

sides.position: Pārthasārathi: no — release has no cognition and no bliss; it is like dreamless sleep without return, a human goal because pain ceases; Kumārila: release is not an enjoyment of pleasure, which would be a perishable heaven.
arguments: Śāstradīpikā mokṣavāda; ŚV sambandhākṣepaparihāra 105–107.

sides.position: Some Bhāṭṭas (reported in the Śāstradīpikā): yes — the self's innate bliss, overpowered in saṃsāra, becomes manifest and is enjoyed through the mind in release; Kumārila's verse states another's view.
No — scripture does not make known accomplished things, and no supreme bliss is experienced by the embodied; release is valuable as the end of sorrow.
Yes — liberation is the realization of Brahman, whose nature is bliss.

historical_debates.name: Vātsyāyana against 'some' who hold eternal pleasure in liberation
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Nyāya: no means of knowledge proves eternal pleasure.

historical_debates.name: Bhāsarvajña's dissent
historical_debates.accounts: Nyāyasāra; Nyāyabhūṣaṇa
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: remained a minority view in Nyāya

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint / terminological: Nyāya denies pleasure as an adventitious quality produced by contact with objects; Advaita affirms bliss as the self's nature, not a produced quality — the two may partly talk past each other.
P1-level: Advaita could read Nyāya's account as describing liberation negatively from the empirical standpoint.
The Śāstradīpikā itself notes that on either view release is a human goal and differs from saṃsāra by the absence of pain.
P1-level: Advaita's bliss belongs to the absolute self, not to an experience of a knower — a reading the Mīmāṃsakas reject.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Mainstream Nyāya explicitly rejects that the self is by nature conscious or blissful and rejects Bhāsarvajña's view; Advaita rejects a liberation without consciousness. The reconciliation is not accepted by either.

question: Should blood offerings (bali) be made to the Goddess?

sides.position: (Kālikā Purāṇa) The Goddess is pleased by offerings; by them liberation and heaven are won and a king conquers his enemies; mantra-purified blood becomes nectar (67.1-12; 67.19-22). The same text restricts them: brāhmaṇas must not offer wine or certain victims, a human offering needs the king's permission, and pumpkin, sugarcane or spirits are 'equal to' a victim (67.23; 67.46-52; 67.113-117).
(Kālīvilāsa) In the Kali age worship is to be performed in the paśu disposition, with pure food and without meat (nirāmiṣa) (4.3).

(Vaiṣṇava) Killing animals is not true worship; the Bhāgavata warns that animals slain in sacrifice await their slayer in the next world (Bhāgavata 4.25.7-8, recalled), and the Goddess is Kṛṣṇa's power acting by his will (Brahmasaṃhitā 5.44); Bengal Vaiṣṇavas reject bali.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the Kālikā Purāṇa enjoins what the Vaiṣṇava and paśu-bhāva positions forbid.
candidate_readings: P4-stage / adhikāra: the Kālikā Purāṇa itself grades offerings by class and permits substitutes; the substitutes (anukalpa) could be read as the tradition's own path for those who will not kill.
P7-arthavada: the promise of liberation through bali (67.5) as praise of the rite rather than doctrine of liberation.
Not reconcilable while one side holds killing to be an offering and the other a sin (ahiṃsā).
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Kāmākhyā tradition holds bali to be enjoined by scripture; Vaiṣṇavas (and Jains and Buddhists) reject any reconciliation that allows killing.

notes: Related: dsp:animal-sacrifice-epic (U05). The Bhāgavata verse number is recalled, not checked.

question: Must one hold a prātimokṣa vow to take the bodhisattva vow?

sides.position: Only those who always keep one of the seven kinds of prātimokṣa vow have the fortune for the bodhisattva vow, not others.
arguments: The bodhisattva vow is built on the ethics of restraint.

sides.position: There are two bodhisattva-vow traditions: the one from Asaṅga (Cittamātra) requires a prior prātimokṣa vow; the one from Nāgārjuna and Śāntideva (Madhyamaka) can be given to anyone with the aspiration; each is to be conferred by its own rite (Sakya Paṇḍita).
arguments: Different rites for different recipients; do not mix the procedures.

reconciliation.explanation: Atiśa's condition applies to the rite of the Bodhisattvabhūmi (Asaṅga's tradition), which is the rite he names; the Madhyamaka rite has different entry conditions.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: A strict reading of Atiśa's verse makes the condition general.

notes: The Sakya side is recalled; chapter reference approximate.

question: Does the liberated (who reached the Brahma-world by meditation) have a body and senses (BS 4.4.10–12)?

sides.position: Bādari: no body.
Jaimini: a body, since scripture speaks of optional multiple forms.

reconciliation.explanation: Bādarāyaṇa (4.4.12) holds both, by choice, like the twelve-day rite that is both a session and a sacrifice — the sūtra's own synthesis.

question: What is Bön's relation to Buddhism: an independent older revelation, or a Tibetan religion that took over Buddhist doctrine?

sides.position: Bön is the teaching of Tönpa Shenrab, a fully enlightened teacher of Ölmo Lungring in Tagzig, far older than Śākyamuni; it reached Tibet through Zhang Zhung, was persecuted and hidden, and recovered as treasure; its parallels with Buddhism reflect one truth or Buddhist borrowing from Bön.
arguments: The biographies (Dodü, Zermig, Zijid) and the histories (Shardza's Treasury of Good Sayings).
An oral Dzogchen lineage (Zhang Zhung Nyengyü) never interrupted.

sides.position: Buddhist historians (e.g. Thuken's Crystal Mirror of Tenets, early 19th c.) describe Bön as a pre-Buddhist religion of rites and spirits that later 'transformed' itself by adopting Buddhist scriptures; Buddhist accounts of Samye report Bön priests defeated and exiled.
arguments: Three phases: revealed, deviant and transformed Bön.
Parallel scriptures and terminology are taken as evidence of copying.
sides.notes: An opponent's report of Bön (reported_by_opponent: the Buddhist historians).

reconciliation.explanation: Both traditions insist on distinct identities; P2 could present the shared Dzogchen as one truth from two standpoints, but that would erase a distinction both sides insist on — not yet reconciled.
candidate_readings: Two independent lineages converging on the same Great Perfection (P2 reading, rejected by both as a statement of origin).
Mutual borrowing over centuries (neither tradition accepts this fully).
Bön as the older source (Bön position).
Bön as derivative (Buddhist polemical position).
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Bön rejects being classified as Buddhism or as derivative; Buddhist polemicists reject Bön's antiquity claims.

notes: Optional (Bön).

question: Does Brahman itself transform into the world, and if so does it change?

sides.position: Bhāskara (and Bhartṛprapañca): Brahman really transforms into the world through its power; the effect is real, different and non-different from the cause.
arguments: BS 1.4.26 'ātmakṛteḥ pariṇāmāt'
BS 2.1.14 teaches non-difference of a real effect

sides.position: Vallabha: Brahman becomes the world without change (avikṛta-pariṇāma), as gold in ornaments; creation is manifestation (āvirbhāva).
arguments: Brahman as locus of contradictory attributes can both transform and remain unchanged

sides.position: Jīva / Caitanya: only the Lord's external power transforms (śakti-pariṇāma); the Lord remains unchanged like the touchstone that yields gold; vivarta is rejected.
arguments: the sūtras teach pariṇāma; Śaṅkara's vivarta departs from Vyāsa

sides.position: Advaita: a real transformation would make Brahman changeable and composite; the world is an apparent transformation (vivarta) of Brahman, a real transformation (pariṇāma) only of māyā.
arguments: scripture calls Brahman partless and changeless
'the modification is only a name' (Chāndogya 6.1.4)

reconciliation.explanation: not yet reconciled: the pariṇāma schools and Advaita disagree on whether the world's reality is ultimate.
candidate_readings: P1-level: Advaita itself admits pariṇāma of māyā at the vyāvahārika level — rejected by all four pariṇāma schools, for whom the world is not merely conventional
Gauḍīya śakti-pariṇāma and Vallabha's avikṛta-pariṇāma as convergent answers to Advaita's objection of change in Brahman (a partial convergence among the Vaiṣṇava schools)
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Bhāskara, Vallabha and the Gauḍīyas reject any reading that assigns the world to a lower level of reality; Advaita rejects real change in Brahman.

question: Is Brahman (God) the material cause of the world, or only its efficient cause?

sides.position: Both: Brahman with souls and matter as its subtle body is the material cause, and as their self the efficient cause; the change belongs to the body, not to Brahman's essence.
arguments: 'by knowing one, all is known'

sides.position: Both, but as the substrate of an apparent transformation (vivarta-upādāna): the world appears on Brahman through māyā.
Only efficient: prakṛti is the material cause; Viṣṇu, eternally distinct, rules it.
Only efficient: God arranges eternal atoms, which are the material cause.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: 'material cause' under different analyses of cause (substrate of change, of appearance, of arrangement)
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Each school holds its analysis of causation to be required by scripture; Dvaita rejects any material causality of God as compromising his changelessness.

notes: Only the Viśiṣṭādvaita side is anchored in U14 teachings; the others are stated in outline for their owners (U13, U15, U11) to anchor.

question: Why did Viṣṇu appear as the Buddha (and how are the Buddhist and Jain teachings to be regarded)?

sides.position: To delude the enemies of the gods and lead them away from the Veda (BhP 1.3.24; VP 3.17-18 Māyāmoha; Agni 16).
Later Vaiṣṇava poetry (Jayadeva's daśāvatāra hymn) praises the Buddha avatāra as compassion condemning animal sacrifice.
arguments: Gīta Govinda 1 (U25 owns)

sides.position: The Buddha is the fully awakened teacher of the true dharma, not an avatāra of Viṣṇu.
arguments: Buddhist self-understanding (U36)

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the Purāṇic account is an opponent's report; the Buddhist tradition rejects the avatāra framing altogether.
candidate_readings: P6-upāya: the Purāṇic 'delusion' as a skilful means for beings of a certain temperament (a Purāṇic reading, rejected by Buddhists).
Two Vaiṣṇava readings (deluding vs compassionate) recorded side by side.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Buddhist and Jain traditions reject both the avatāra identification and the charge of delusion.

notes: The Jayadeva side is cited under lin:alvar only as the nearest registry Vaiṣṇava-poet lineage; U25 owns Jayadeva.

queries: cited refs located in local e-texts
checks.note: Purāṇic side located (BhP 1.3.24; VP 3.17.41-3.18.24; AgP 16.1-4). The Jayadeva and Buddhist sides are other units' and were not re-checked here.

question: Do insentient things (walls, tiles, grasses) have buddha-nature or preach the Dharma?

sides.position: Nanyang Huizhong: the buddha-mind is walls, tiles and pebbles; the insentient preach the Dharma, heard when free of the feelings of consciousness.
(Objection voiced by a monk, citing the Nirvāṇa-sūtra) Buddha-nature is what is apart from walls and insentient things; buddha-nature is permanent, mind impermanent.

texts.ref: as cited in Jingde chuandeng lu juan 28

sides.position: Dōgen: whole being is buddha-nature; impermanence is buddha-nature.

reconciliation.explanation: Huizhong's own answer: 'deluded, they differ; awakened, they do not' — like ice and water — distinguishes the standpoint of delusion from that of awakening.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Scholastic readers of the Nirvāṇa-sūtra keep the distinction between sentient buddha-nature and insentient things; Tiantai (Zhanran) argued the insentient have buddha-nature on other grounds (U54).

question: Is buddha-nature a true self (permanent, blissful, pure, not empty of qualities) or another name for emptiness?

sides.position: Buddha-nature is the true self: 'self means the tathāgatagarbha'; the dharmakāya has the perfection of self; the garbha is not empty of the inseparable buddha-qualities.
arguments: 'No-self is saṃsāra, self is the Tathāgata' (Mahāparinirvāṇa juan 2).
'Self means the tathāgatagarbha' (juan 7).
Śrīmālā 9 and 12; RGV 1.35.
Aṅgulimālīya.

sides.position: The tathāgatagarbha is not the self of the tīrthikas: the buddhas teach it meaning emptiness, the reality-limit, nirvāṇa, the unborn, so that the foolish may not fear no-self; its purpose is to remove five faults.
arguments: Laṅkāvatāra p. 33.
RGV 1.156-157: taught to remove discouragement, contempt, etc.

sides.position: (East Asian reading from the same sūtra) Buddha-nature is the emptiness of the highest meaning, which sees both empty and non-empty — the middle way.
arguments: Mahāparinirvāṇa juan 27.

reconciliation.explanation: The texts themselves distinguish levels — the Mahāparinirvāṇa separates worldly and supramundane 'self', and the Laṅkāvatāra and RGV state the teaching's purpose — so 'self' and 'no-self' refer to different objects (the dharmakāya's qualities vs the imagined self of the aggregates).
reconciliation.detail: Under P1 the 'self' of the garbha is the ultimate-level perfection of the dharmakāya and 'no-self' denies the self imagined in the aggregates; under P6 the Laṅkāvatāra says the garbha-teaching is skillful means. What remains open is whether the garbha's 'self' is itself definitive (P5) — see dsp:which-turning-is-definitive.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Jonang and many East Asian readers hold the self-language definitive, not skillful means; Gelug holds buddha-nature to be the mind's emptiness and rejects any non-empty absolute; Theravāda rejects any self at all (dsp:is-there-a-self).

question: May monks reside permanently in temples and manage their property?

sides.position: The temple-dwelling monks (as reported by their opponents): residence in and care of temples serves the tradition and the laity.
arguments: Custom of the time; royal patronage

sides.position: No: monks must live in lodgings given by laypeople, wander, and own nothing, as the Āgamas prescribe.
arguments: The canonical rules of wandering and non-possession
Haribhadra's criticism of the temple-dwellers

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled; the temple-dwellers' side survives mainly in their opponents' accounts.
candidate_readings: P4-stage: settled clerics serving temples and wandering mendicants as different roles — the later yati/mendicant distinction partly institutionalized this
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The reformers held temple-dwelling to be a breach of the vows, not a different role.

historical_debates.name: Debate at Aṇahilapāṭaka
historical_debates.accounts: Kharatara accounts: before King Durlabharāja, Jineśvara defeated the temple-dwellers and won the epithet 'kharatara'.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Vasativāsī monks allowed to reside in the capital; origin of the Kharatara Gaccha.

question: Can all beings attain buddhahood, or are there beings (icchantikas, those without lineage) who never will?

sides.position: All sentient beings have buddha-nature, including the icchantika; there is no fixed icchantika; all will attain buddhahood.
arguments: All beings are tathāgatagarbhas because the dharmakāya pervades them, suchness is undivided and the lineage is present (RGV 1.27-28).
'All beings have buddha-nature — even the icchantikas; because they will surely attain unsurpassed awakening in the future it is said all have it' (Mahāparinirvāṇa juan 27).
One who understands the four alternatives should not insist that the icchantika definitely lacks it (juan 36).
The Lotus: there is only one vehicle and all who hear become buddhas.

sides.position: Beings have distinct lineages (gotra); some belong to the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha lineage and some have no lineage (agotra) and do not attain buddhahood; the teaching of universal buddha-nature was given with a hidden intention.
arguments: The Laṅkāvatāra lists five lineages, the fifth being 'no lineage'.

The icchantika who has abandoned the roots of merit by rejecting the bodhisattva collection does not enter nirvāṇa (Laṅkāvatāra p. 28) — though it adds that the Tathāgata's power may revive his roots.
The Saṃdhinirmocana (ch. 7) says the śrāvaka of fixed lineage cannot be led to awakening even by all buddhas; the one vehicle was taught with an intention (from memory, chapter-level).

sides.position: Faxian's six-fascicle Nirvāṇa Sūtra (418) and its first Chinese readers: icchantikas are excluded from buddha-nature.
arguments: The early part of the Mahāparinirvāṇa says icchantikas, having cut off the roots of good, lack buddha-nature (in the sense of wholesome qualities) (T374 juan 26 retains this).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: each side uses the tradition's own P5/P6 hermeneutic to make the other's teaching provisional, so the principle cannot decide between them.
candidate_readings: P5 (Yogācāra reading): 'all have buddha-nature' is neyārtha, spoken to encourage beings of indeterminate lineage.
P5/P6 (Tathāgatagarbha and Tiantai reading): the five-lineage teaching is a skillful means; the one vehicle and universal buddha-nature are nītārtha.
P4 (Mahāparinirvāṇa juan 36 and Laṅkāvatāra p. 28 themselves): 'icchantika' names a present condition, not an eternal nature — the Tathāgata's power can revive the roots of good.
P1 (Faxiang's own distinction, reported from memory): buddha-nature as principle (lixing) all beings have; buddha-nature as practice (xingxing) some lack.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Tiantai/Tendai and Huayan reject any being permanently without buddhahood; the Faxiang/Hossō tradition rejects universal attainment as the definitive teaching.

historical_debates.name: Daosheng on the icchantika
historical_debates.accounts: Daosheng taught, against the six-fascicle Nirvāṇa Sūtra, that icchantikas too can become buddhas and was expelled from the capital's saṅgha; when Dharmakṣema's 40-fascicle version arrived it contained that teaching.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Chinese accounts: Daosheng vindicated.

historical_debates.name: The 'three-one' controversy (Saichō and Tokuitsu)
historical_debates.accounts: Saichō (Tendai) defended the one vehicle and universal buddha-nature; Tokuitsu (Hossō) defended the three vehicles and the five lineages.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Each school claimed victory; Tendai's position became dominant in Japan.

question: Does the statement 'all things are empty' refute itself?

sides.position: If all things lack own-nature, the statement 'all things lack own-nature' also lacks it and cannot negate anything; if it has own-nature, not all things are empty. Either way the thesis fails.
arguments: An unreal statement cannot negate.
A real statement is a counter-example.

sides.position: My words are dependently arisen and so empty, yet they function, as empty carts and pots do their work; they negate as one magical man stops another. And I have no thesis, so the faults of a thesis do not touch me.
arguments: Emptiness is not non-existence but dependent origination (VV 22).
Empty things still function (VV 22–23).
No thesis is advanced (VV 29).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the Madhyamaka answer relies on the two truths, which the realist does not grant.
candidate_readings: P1-level: words function conventionally without own-nature, so the statement works at the conventional level (Nāgārjuna's own answer).
P2-standpoint: from the realist's standpoint a functioning statement must be real; from the Mādhyamika's, function does not require own-nature — two standpoints, not one truth-claim.
No-thesis reading (VV 29): the Mādhyamika only shows the opponent's inconsistencies, so no self-refuting thesis is asserted.

question: Can every soul eventually be liberated, or are some souls by nature never to be liberated?

sides.position: Souls are of three innate classes: those fit for liberation, those who transmigrate forever, and those fit for eternal blinding darkness; this gradation is beginningless and unalterable, and liberation and darkness are both final.
arguments: the classification is stated in doctrinal treatises (Tattvasaṅkhyāna, Tattvaviveka) and in MBTN 1
fitness is intrinsic; no means can alter it (MBTN 1.95)
scripture speaks of eternal darkness for the enemies of Hari

sides.position: Every soul is in truth Brahman; bondage is ignorance, and any soul that gains the knowledge of identity is liberated; no self is by nature excluded from that knowledge.
arguments: the self of all is one Brahman
liberation is the removal of ignorance, open to all who are qualified

sides.position: All bound souls are capable of liberation through the Lord's grace, won by devotion or surrender; the tradition knows no class of souls eternally excluded from it.
arguments: the Lord's grace is universal in scope
surrender (prapatti) is open to all

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Dvaita rejects both readings: fitness is 'beginningless and endless, and no one can alter it' (MBTN 1.95), and the classification appears in treatises of classification, not in praise or blame. The other schools reject Dvaita's premise of intrinsically unliberable souls.

candidate_readings.reading: The 'classes' describe stages of spiritual maturity, not fixed natures.
The passages on eternal darkness are hortatory warnings (praise and blame).

notes: An analogous Jain doctrine (souls 'incapable of liberation', abhavya) is noted as a term equivalence, not as a side. The Advaita and Viśiṣṭādvaita positions are summarized from general knowledge.

question: Can those who have committed the five grave offences or slandered the Dharma be born in the Pure Land?

sides.position: The eighteenth vow excludes those who commit the five grave offences and slander the true Dharma (the Sanskrit likewise).
The Contemplation Sūtra's lowest grade: one who has committed the five offences and ten evils is born by ten recitations at death.
(Tanluan) One guilty of both offences and slander cannot be born; one who committed the offences without slandering can, since slander rejects the very Dharma.
(Shandao) The vow's exclusion is a gate of restraint to deter; once committed, these too are embraced.
(Shinran) Even the 'difficult to cure' — slanderers, grave offenders, icchantikas — are healed, as Ajātaśatru was.

reconciliation.explanation: Shandao reads the exclusion as a skilful deterrent (gate of restraint) and the lower-grade birth as the gate of embrace — the tradition's own reconciliation by skilful means.
reconciliation.detail: Tanluan's earlier solution (distinguishing slander) is retained as a reading of degree.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Tanluan's position that slanderers cannot be born is not the same as Shandao's; the two readings are recorded side by side.

question: Can practices other than the nenbutsu bring birth in the Pure Land?

sides.position: Yes: the three meritorious acts, the sixteen contemplations and all good roots dedicated to birth lead there (the sūtras; Chinese masters).

(Hōnen) They are set aside; the primal vow's practice is the nenbutsu alone. (Chōsai, as reported) The various practices too are vowed in the primal vow. (Benchō's line, as usually stated) They can bring birth but are not the vow's own practice.
They lead only to the transformed land (19th vow).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled among Hōnen's disciples' lines.
candidate_readings: P4-stage: other practices for those unable to entrust exclusively (Shinran's provisional gate)
P6-upaya: other practices taught to lead beings toward the nenbutsu (Senchakushū 4's first reading)

notes: Positions of Chōsai and Benchō given in general terms only (low confidence).

question: Can an unconscious pradhāna, without a conscious director, bring forth and order the world?

sides.position: Yes: prakṛti acts spontaneously for puruṣa's purpose; no Lord is needed or established.
arguments: As unconscious milk flows for the calf, pradhāna acts for puruṣa's liberation (SK 57); as people act to satisfy a longing (SK 58).

The conjunction of the seeing and the moving is like that of the lame and the blind (SK 21); the subtle body acts like an actor for puruṣa's purpose (SK 42); the instruments are made to act by no one (SK 31).
Pradhāna's activity is like milk, spontaneous like a servant's, drawn on by beginningless karma (SS 3.58–63); governance by mere proximity, like a magnet (SS 1.96).
Īśvara is not established (SS 1.92–99; 5.2–12); effects depend on ahaṃkāra, not Īśvara (SS 6.64); the attributeless cannot produce what has guṇas (Gauḍapāda on SK 61).

sides.position: No: the inferred pradhāna cannot be the cause, because an unconscious cause cannot produce orderly arrangement or activity.
arguments: Orderly arrangement is impossible for the inferred cause (BS 2.2.1), and activity too (2.2.2).
Milk and water flow under a conscious being's direction (2.2.3).
The lame-and-blind or magnet analogies fail (2.2.7); the guṇas in equilibrium cannot become principal and subordinate (2.2.8); the doctrine is incoherent (2.2.10).

sides.position: No: effects such as the world require an intelligent maker (Īśvara) as their efficient cause.
arguments: Udayana's arguments for a world-knowing, imperishable maker from effects, arrangement, support and other marks (Nyāyakusumāñjali 5.1).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: whether a conscious agent is required is the point at issue.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint (causal): prakṛti as material cause and a Lord as efficient cause — the theistic-Sāṃkhya reading; rejected by classical Sāṃkhya (SS 1.92) and by Advaita, for which Brahman is both material and efficient cause.
P2-standpoint (purpose): Sāṃkhya's teleology 'for puruṣa' already locates the orienting factor in consciousness (puruṣa's presence), which Vedānta places in the Lord.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Classical Sāṃkhya denies that any Īśvara is established; Vedānta and Nyāya deny that the milk and lame-blind analogies apply without a conscious director.

question: Did the original Jain scripture survive?

sides.position: Yes, largely: the eleven Aṅgas and the other Āgamas were preserved through the councils of Pāṭaliputra, Mathurā and Valabhī and written down under Devarddhigaṇi; only the Dṛṣṭivāda with the Pūrvas was lost.
arguments: The councils recovered what memory held
The twelve-limbed canon is eternal in meaning and re-proclaimed by every Jina

sides.position: No: knowledge of the Aṅgas and Pūrvas dwindled until 683 years after the nirvāṇa no complete Aṅga was known; only parts survive in the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama and Kaṣāyapāhuḍa; the Śvetāmbara Āgamas are later compositions of a group that had relaxed the discipline.
arguments: The line of 3 omniscients, 5 śrutakevalins, 11 daśapūrvins, 5 ekādaśāṅgins and 4 ācārāṅgins
Dharasena's transmission to Puṣpadanta and Bhūtabali
The Śvetāmbara texts contain teachings (women's liberation, the kevalin's eating) the Digambaras hold false

sides.position: The old canon survives in a form the Yāpanīyas accepted and cited (Āvaśyaka, Chedasūtras, niryuktis).
arguments: Aparājita's citations

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: a question of transmission history on which the accounts differ.
candidate_readings: The two accounts may describe the same decline from different sides: the Śvetāmbaras preserved a recited canon with admitted losses, the Digambaras stressed the loss and preserved other portions
Scholarly account (labelled, not a reconciliation): the Śvetāmbara canon contains old material of many periods; the Digambara āgamas are independent early works
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Digambaras reject the authenticity of the Śvetāmbara Āgamas outright; the Śvetāmbaras reject the Digambara claim of total loss.

question: Is purity and worth determined by birth into a class (varṇa), or by conduct?

sides.position: The brahmin is the highest class, born from the mouth of the cosmic Person / of Brahmā, Brahmā's heir; the classes are ordained by birth, and purity belongs to the brahmin class.
arguments: The Puruṣasūkta derives the brāhmaṇa from the Person's mouth (RV 10.90.12).
The Dharmaśāstra assigns duties by birth (Manusmṛti 1.31, 1.87–91).
As stated by brahmin interlocutors in the suttas: 'only brahmins are pure, only brahmins are Brahmā's sons' (DN 27; MN 93).

sides.position: One is a brahmin or an outcaste not by birth but by deeds; all four classes can do good and evil and all can be purified; the classes arose from occupations; the Dhamma, not birth, is best among people.
arguments: Brahmin women are seen to menstruate and give birth (DN 27; MN 93).
Plants and animals differ by species, humans do not; names follow occupations (MN 98).
Fire from any wood burns alike; all can develop love and wash off dirt (MN 93).
The true brahmin is the one who has nothing and clings to nothing (Dhp 396; Snp 1.7).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the Buddhist texts deny that birth confers purity, which the Brahmanical sources affirm.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: the Brahmanical varṇa as a ritual and social order (ethical-social standpoint) versus spiritual worth by conduct (seeker standpoint) — the Brahmanical tradition itself sometimes defines the true brahmin by conduct (e.g. the Yakṣapraśna, Vajrasūcī Upaniṣad)
P1-level: birth-based duties as conventional, liberation as open to all — but the suttas also reject birth-based rank conventionally
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The suttas reject birth-status even at the conventional level (DN 27, MN 93); orthodox Dharmaśāstra holds varṇa by birth as dharma. Neither accepts a reconciliation that makes the other's claim merely a standpoint.

historical_debates.name: Dialogues with brahmins
historical_debates.accounts: DN 3, DN 4, DN 27, MN 93, MN 98 / Snp 3.9 (Buddhist accounts only)
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: In the Buddhist accounts the brahmins concede or become followers.

notes: Related to dsp:women-caste-liberation (U50).

question: May people of low birth know and expound the meaning of scripture and approach God on equal terms?

sides.position: Vedic study, the exposition of the Veda's meaning and certain rights of worship belong to the twice-born by birth (adhikāra); the children of a sannyāsin who returned to household life are outcaste; a śūdra must not teach the Veda's meaning.
arguments: Varṇa duties and rights are set by śruti and smṛti.
Purity rules protect the rites and the temple.

texts.ref: passim (rules of adhikāra; not cited verse by verse here)

sides.note: This side is known here chiefly as the Vārkarī hagiographies report it (Paiṭhaṇ brahmins; Rāmeśvar Bhaṭṭ) — reported by the opposing side.

sides.position: Before God birth counts for nothing: the name is open to all; the devotee, whatever his birth, knows the Veda's meaning; the low-born saints are revered as equals; the Gītā itself promises the highest to women, vaiśyas and śūdras who take refuge.
arguments: BhG 9.32 as expounded by Jñāneśvar: rivers lose their names in the ocean.
The sugarcane is crooked, its juice is not (Cokhāmeḷā).
'We alone know the Veda's meaning; the others carry its burden' (Tukārām).
The buffalo that recited the Veda shows one Self in all.

historical_debates.name: The siblings before the Paiṭhaṇ brahmins
historical_debates.accounts: Bhaktavijaya; Nāmdev's abhaṅgas
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Vārkarī account: the buffalo recites the Veda and the brahmins issue a letter of purification (śuddhi-patra).

historical_debates.name: Rāmeśvar Bhaṭṭ and Tukārām
historical_debates.accounts: Bhaktavijaya; Tukārām Gāthā
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Vārkarī account: the notebooks rise from the Indrāyaṇī and Rāmeśvar becomes a disciple.

historical_debates.name: Cokhāmeḷā's exclusion from the Paṇḍharpūr temple
historical_debates.accounts: Cokhāmeḷā's abhaṅgas
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: His samādhi stands at the temple's gate; he is revered by all Vārkarīs.

historical_debates.name: Temple-entry movement at Paṇḍharpūr (recent)
historical_debates.accounts: Sāne Guruji's fast for opening the Viṭṭhala temple to Dalits (recent; recalled, verify)
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: temple opened to all castes

reconciliation.explanation: The orthodox rules govern entitlement to Vedic ritual and study; the saints' claim concerns the path of the name and devotion, which scripture itself (BhG 9.32) opens to all.
reconciliation.detail: Recorded as a partial reconciliation of scope only: the two sides legislate for different paths. It does not settle who may expound scripture, temple access, or social rank.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Vārkarī saints deny that birth confers any spiritual rank at all, including in understanding the Veda; orthodox authorities historically rejected low-caste exposition and temple entry. Neither side is recorded as accepting this reconciliation.

notes: Related to the fixed dispute dsp:women-caste-liberation (U50).

question: Does the effect pre-exist in its cause (satkārya), is it newly produced (asatkārya/ārambha), is it an apparent transformation of an unchanging cause (vivarta), a real manifestation of consciousness (ābhāsa), a transformation of God that leaves him unchanged (avikṛta-pariṇāma), or dependently arisen and ultimately unarisen?

sides.position: The effect exists in its material cause before it is produced (satkārya): because what does not exist cannot be produced; because a definite material cause is taken for a definite effect; because not everything arises from everything; because a capable cause produces only what it is capable of; because the effect has the nature of its cause. Production is manifestation.

Past and future exist in their own form, differing in their time-paths; change is transformation of property, time-mark and state in an enduring substrate; the instrumental cause does not set the material causes going but only removes the obstruction, as a farmer breaches a dyke.

The effect is a new thing, non-existent before production (asatkārya, ārambhavāda): before it is produced the fruit is not existent in the Sāṃkhya sense, for existence and non-existence are opposed; it comes about from inherent, non-inherent and instrumental causes and is the counterpositive of its prior absence. Nor does existence arise from non-existence as such (the sprout from the destroyed seed).
From the absence of the cause follows the absence of the effect, not the reverse; a thing before it is produced is non-existent (prior absence) — the effect is a newly made whole.

The effect is non-different from its cause, 'a verbal handle, a name' — as pots are only clay (CU 6.1.4; BS 2.1.14). Brahman is both material and efficient cause; the world is its apparent transformation (vivarta), not a real modification (vikāra): the snake is only the rope. From the highest standpoint nothing whatever is born.

Brahman is both the material and the efficient cause; the world is non-different from Brahman as pots from clay, but the effect is a real state of Brahman, whose body is the sentient and non-sentient; real transformation (pariṇāma) touches Brahman's body, not its essence.
Brahman makes itself into the world by real transformation of its power (ātmakṛteḥ pariṇāmāt); the effect is real, both different and non-different from its cause (Bhāskara; Nimbārka).
Brahman, transforming itself, is the material cause of the world, yet this transformation involves no change in Brahman (avikṛta-pariṇāma).

Viṣṇu is the independent cause who creates, maintains, dissolves and controls; the world is real and its material is prakṛti, dependent on him; the doctrine of apparent transformation is refuted, since the witness establishes what is real.

Things that appear in the present as external are possible only if they already exist within consciousness; the Lord, by his will and infinite powers, makes them appear (ābhāsa) — this is his creatorhood. Consciousness, free, is the cause of the universe, which she unfolds on her own screen: a real self-manifestation, not an illusion.

The world, spoken of as 'he, she and it', undergoes origination, maintenance and dissolution, so it has an agent; it resolves into and re-emerges from its cause — Śiva as efficient cause working through real māyā as material.
Formations occur through ignorance and the other conditions; the wheel of becoming has no maker such as a Brahmā: things arise dependently, neither from a self-made nor an other-made cause.

No existent whatever is ever found arisen from itself, from another, from both, or without a cause (MMK 1.1); the effect is neither made of the conditions nor of non-conditions; dependent arising is itself emptiness, and emptiness, dependent origination and the middle way have one meaning.

The existent is endowed at once with origination, cessation and persistence: a thing is in some respect existent and in some respect non-existent before its production. Time, own-nature, destiny, former deeds and human effort, each held one-sidedly as the cause, are wrong views; taken together they are right view.

Brahman, without beginning or end, whose essence is the Word, appears (vivartate) as objects; the world is the Word-principle's appearing (Bhartṛhari — the earliest use of vivarta as a technical term recorded here).
Time, own-nature, fixed order, chance, the elements, the womb and the person are weighed as causes and none suffices; it is the greatness of God in the world by which the wheel of Brahman turns.

historical_debates.name: The commentarial exchange on MMK 1.1
historical_debates.accounts: Buddhapālita-vṛtti 1.1; Prajñāpradīpa 1.1; Prasannapadā 1.1 (see dsp:prasangika-svatantrika)
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Mādhyamikas agree that nothing arises from self, other, both or neither; they differ on how to demonstrate it.

historical_debates.name: Sāṃkhya and its critics on the pre-existent effect (textual)
historical_debates.date: c. early centuries CE onward (scholarly, approximate)
historical_debates.accounts: Sāṃkhyakārikā 9; Nyāyasūtra 4.1.48-50; Madhyamakahṛdaya 6; Brahmasūtra 2.1.14-20 and 2.2.1-10
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Each tradition holds its own account of causation; Vedānta adopts the non-difference of effect from cause while rejecting Sāṃkhya's unconscious pradhāna.

reconciliation.explanation: Partly reconciled by the traditions' own devices: Advaita and Madhyamaka accept causal change or dependent arising at the conventional level while denying real origination ultimately (P1), and the Jains hold the pre-existence and the novelty of the effect true from the substance and mode standpoints (P2); the Sāṃkhya–Nyāya and vivarta–ābhāsa disagreements are not yet reconciled.
reconciliation.detail: P1: Śaṅkara uses the language of transformation for the empirical world and non-difference/vivarta for the ultimate (BSBh 2.1.14; Vedāntasāra's vikāra–vivarta verse); Nāgārjuna negates the four modes of arising while affirming dependent arising as emptiness (MMK 1.1; VV 71). P2: the Jain triad of origination, cessation and persistence (TS 5.30) and Siddhasena's rule that each single cause held one-sidedly is wrong view (Sanmati 3.53) are the Jains' own reconciliation. What remains: whether the effect's pre-existence is literal (Sāṃkhya) or incoherent (Nyāya); whether the world's appearance is real manifestation of consciousness (Kashmir Śaivism) or indeterminable superimposition (Advaita); whether Brahman's transformation is real (Viśiṣṭādvaita, Bhedābheda, Vallabha) or apparent.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Nyāya rejects satkārya outright (NS 4.1.48-50) and Sāṃkhya asatkārya (SK 9); Viśiṣṭādvaita, Bhedābheda, Vallabha and Dvaita deny that the world's transformation is merely apparent (Śrībhāṣya 2.1.15; Anuvyākhyāna 1.4.95-98); Kashmir Śaivism holds manifestation real, not vivarta; Madhyamaka rejects the Jain 'both' as a mode of arising already negated (MMK 1.1).

candidate_readings: P2-standpoint for Sāṃkhya vs Nyāya: satkārya speaks of the material cause's capacity (the substance standpoint), asatkārya of the product as a new whole (the mode standpoint) — rejected by both, each of whom argues the other's thesis is incoherent.

P1-level for Advaita vs Kashmir Śaivism: both deny change in the ultimate consciousness; they differ on whether the appearance is real self-display (ābhāsa) or indeterminable (vivarta) — the Trika insists on the reality of manifestation, Advaita on its sublatability.
P1-level for Advaita vs the theistic Vedāntas: transformation (pariṇāma) true empirically, vivarta true ultimately — rejected by Rāmānuja, Nimbārka, Vallabha and Madhva, who deny degrees of reality.
notes: Scholarly observation (metadata only): the term vivarta is used by Bhartṛhari before its Advaita use.

question: Does the destruction of a conditioned thing have a cause?

sides.position: Impermanence is one of the four real characteristics that acts on each dharma; destruction is characterized, though things are momentary.
No: destruction is causeless and spontaneous; what arises perishes of itself; apparent destruction by fire is non-arising of a similar series.
Some formations are momentary, others endure for a time (Vasumitra).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the Vaibhāṣika holds a real entity where the Sautrāntika sees a designation.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Each side holds the other's account inadequate: the Vaibhāṣika that designations cannot do causal work, the Sautrāntika that the posited entities are unnecessary and unattested in the sūtras.

candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: the characteristic 'impermanence' names what the Sautrāntika calls the thing's own perishing — rejected by both as to the reality of the characteristic.

question: What causes the owner–owned relation between puruṣa and prakṛti? (views recorded in the Sāṃkhya Sūtra)

sides.position: Karma: the relation is caused by karma and is beginningless like seed and sprout (SS 6.67).
Non-discrimination (Pañcaśikha, SS 6.68).
The subtle body (the teacher Sanandana, SS 6.69).

reconciliation.explanation: The sūtra records the three as alternatives without rejecting any; they name the relation's cause at different removes (non-discrimination at the root, karma as its working, the subtle body as its carrier).
reconciliation.detail: Non-discrimination is elsewhere called the cause of the conjunction (SS 1.55) and bondage itself (SS 6.16), which supports reading the three as compatible.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: None recorded in the texts consulted.

question: What occasions the descent of power (śaktipāta): the equality of karma, the maturing of impurity, or the Lord's free will alone?

sides.position: Its time is the equality of the soul's karmas; Śiva waits for that time because of the soul's beginningless karma, yet remains its lord and cause, as the sun is of the opening lotus.
arguments: figurative 'fall'
archer and moving target
sun and lotus

sides.position: Viṣṇu's compassion — his power of grace called śaktipāta — arises for the suffering soul; by his glance its karmas become equal and fall silent, and it is lifted out of saṃsāra.
arguments: grace is the fifth power
robbers and the traveller

sides.position: Abhinavagupta rejects karma-equality and the ripening of impurity as causes: the descent depends on the Lord's independence alone.
arguments: Tantrāloka 13

sides.position: The ripening of mala (malaparipāka) is the occasion; the Lord, not the mala, is the cause.
Both: when the two deeds are balanced (iruviṉaiyoppu) and āṇava has ripened (malaparipākam), grace descends in four grades.

reconciliation.explanation: Under P2 the Kiraṇa's own image (sun and lotus) states the event from the causal standpoint (karma-equality as the time) and the divine standpoint (the Lord as cause); the Ahirbudhnya states it from the divine standpoint, with karma-equality as effect.
reconciliation.detail: The reconciliation covers the Kiraṇa and Ahirbudhnya only. It does not claim the two agree on the direction of causation, nor that the Trika position is included.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Abhinavagupta explicitly rejects karma-equality as a cause of śaktipāta; the Trika therefore objects to any reading that makes it a condition.

notes: The Trika side (TĀ 13) is recorded from memory at chapter level; U19 should add the teaching record.

question: What caused the first schism between the Sthaviras and the Mahāsāṃghikas?

sides.position: Laxity in discipline: the Vajjiputtakas' ten points were rejected at Vesālī; the defeated monks formed the Mahāsaṅgītika and altered the texts.
Doctrine: Mahādeva's five points lowering the arhat divided the Saṅgha under Aśoka.
Vinaya recension: an elder enlarged and rearranged the Vinaya; the great community kept the original.

historical_debates.name: The Council of Vaiśālī
historical_debates.accounts: Cullavagga 12 and the other Vinayas
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: The ten points judged unallowable

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the schools remember different causes for the first division of the Saṅgha.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Each tradition presents its own side as the faithful one and the other as the innovators.

candidate_readings: Historical reading: several successive disputes (the ten points at Vaiśālī, the five points, Vinaya recension) each remembered by the side it justified — the traditions do not frame it so.
P2-standpoint: each account is true from the standpoint of its community's discipline — rejected by each, which regards the other side as having departed from the Dharma-Vinaya.

question: Is recitation of the Buddha's name compatible with Chan?

sides.position: The deluded recite the Buddha's name seeking the West; the awakened purify their own minds — the Pure Land is the pure mind (Platform Sūtra); guarding one's own mind surpasses recollecting another buddha (Xiuxin yao lun).
Joint practice: Chan and recitation together, as advocated by Yongming Yanshou, Zhongfeng Mingben, Yunqi Zhuhong and the Ōbaku school; Musang opened his assemblies with recitation.

reconciliation.explanation: Recitation as a method for devotional temperaments and as a huatou ('who recites?') within Chan practice.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Pure Land schools (U43) hold rebirth through Amitābha's vow to be the point, not a mind-only reading; some Chan teachers reject mixing the two.

question: Is Chan a special transmission outside the scriptural teachings, or one with them?

sides.position: A special transmission outside the teachings, not established on words and letters; the twelve divisions of scripture are only expressions; one must not seek the meaning in words.
arguments: Flower sermon; Linji's dismissal of names and phrases; Dahui is said to have burned the Blue Cliff blocks.

sides.position: Chan and the teachings coincide: Zongmi correlates the three Chan tenets with three doctrinal teachings; Yanshou takes the one mind as the source of both.
Hyujeong: Chan is the Buddha's mind and the teachings his words; first understand through the teachings, then enter Chan through the live word.
The Platform Sūtra: those who say 'do not use words' slander the scriptures, for 'not using' is itself words.

reconciliation.explanation: Teachings as the provisional means and first stage, Chan as direct realization of what they point to (Hyujeong's sequence).
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Strict Linji voices reject subordinating Chan to doctrine; doctrinal schools (e.g. Tiantai) reject the claim of a separate transmission.

question: Should Chan meditation and Pure Land recitation be practised together?

sides.position: Yes: both return to the one source; Chan is the Chan of Pure Land and Pure Land the Pure Land of Chan; practise one gate deeply; all good practices share one end.
Mixing practices loses birth; exclusive practice alone is right.
Recitation is for those of lesser capacity, or a huatou; seeking a Buddha outside is contrary to seeing one's nature (as reported).

reconciliation.explanation: Zhuhong's 'return to the source is not two, expedient gates are many' reconciles by path, while urging depth in one gate.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Shandao's line (and Jōdo-shū) warns that mixed practice fails; Chan purists deny the need.

question: Is Chöd — a practice first taught by a Tibetan woman and concerned with spirits and the gift of the body — authentic Buddhadharma with an Indian source?

sides.position: Chöd is the practical application of the Perfection of Wisdom: its view is that of the sūtras, its instructions come in part from the Indian siddha Padampa Sangye and from Āryadeva the Brahmin's Grand Poem, and Machig is the emanation of the Great Mother. Indian scholars who came to test her accepted it, and it is the one Dharma that went from Tibet to India.
arguments: The root texts are titled instructions of the Perfection of Wisdom and apply its view of emptiness.
The father lineage runs from Padampa Sangye.
The tradition's account of the Indian scholars' test and acceptance.

sides.party: Tibetan critics applying the criterion that authentic Dharma must have an Indian original (known here chiefly as reported in the Chöd tradition's own narratives; critics not named with confidence)
sides.position: A practice composed in Tibet, lacking an Indian tantra or sūtra as its source and centred on dealings with spirits, cannot be accepted as the Buddha's teaching merely on the authority of a Tibetan founder.
arguments: The general Tibetan criterion that doctrines must be traced to an Indian source.
Suspicion of practices associated with spirit-dealing and wandering yogins.

historical_debates.name: The Indian scholars' test of Machig (tradition's account)
historical_debates.accounts: Recorded in the Chöd tradition's own biographies of Machig.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: The Chöd tradition: the Indians accepted her teaching and took it to India.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled; the critics' side is known only through the defending tradition.
candidate_readings: P5-neyartha: authenticity judged by agreement with the definitive Perfection of Wisdom rather than by place of origin (the Chöd tradition's own argument).
P6-upaya: the spirit-dealing form as skillful means for cutting self-clinging in Tibetan conditions.
Historical question (origin) and doctrinal question (conformity with the sūtras) treated separately.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Critics insisting on an Indian original would not accept a doctrinal-conformity criterion alone.

notes: Low confidence on the critics' side; it is recorded so that the debate named in the coverage brief has an entry, and should be sourced before any reconciliation.

question: Is the mind a series of momentary cognitions, or one enduring mind with many objects?

sides.position: The mind is one, has many objects and endures; properties inhere in an enduring property-bearer.
arguments: If the mind were momentary and tied to one object per cognition, every mind would be one-pointed and none distracted (YBh 1.32).
Memory and the enjoyment of karma require one experiencer (YBh 1.32, 3.14).
The self-experienced 'I who saw now touch' requires one cognizer (YBh 1.32).

sides.position: All conditioned things, cognition included, are momentary; continuity is that of a series (santāna), not of an enduring substrate.
arguments: Momentariness follows from destruction being uncaused (Buddhist argument).
sides.note: From memory; refs to check. YBh 1.32 reports the view as an opponent's.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: substance (dravyārthika) vs mode (paryāyārthika) descriptions of mind.
Leave distinct: Vyāsa explicitly refutes momentariness.

notes: Related to dsp:is-there-a-self (U50).

question: Is consciousness a product of the combined elements of the body?

sides.position: No: consciousness is not found in the elements separately, nor in combination; puruṣa, other than the body, exists.
arguments: SS 3.20–22, 5.129, 6.1–3; SK 17 (aggregates exist for another).

sides.position: Yes: consciousness arises from the combination of elements, as intoxicating power from ingredients.
arguments: Stated as the opponent's view in SS 3.22; Cārvāka's own sūtras survive only in quotations.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled.
candidate_readings: P1-level: the materialist account as a description of embodied consciousness only (rejected by both).
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Sāṃkhya holds puruṣa distinct from all elements; Cārvāka denies any self beyond the body.

question: Is it the same consciousness that runs and wanders through the rounds of rebirth?

sides.position: (Sāti) 'As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this same consciousness that runs and wanders on, not another' — the one that speaks and feels and experiences the results of deeds.
(The Buddha) Consciousness is dependently arisen; without a condition there is no arising of consciousness; it is reckoned by its condition as fire by its fuel.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled as a doctrinal question beyond the text: the sutta itself rejects Sāti's view.
candidate_readings: P1-level: continuity of a conditioned series spoken of conventionally (later Theravāda: rebirth-linking consciousness as a new moment conditioned by the last)
The Pudgalavāda 'person' as the carrier (U38, dsp:pudgala)
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Theravāda holds Sāti's view to be a wrong view outright, not a standpoint.

notes: Intra-Buddhist; linked to dsp:is-there-a-self (U50) and dsp:pudgala (U38).

question: Was the world created, and does it undergo total dissolution?

sides.position: No means of knowledge establishes a first creation or a dissolution of everything; a bodiless Prajāpati could not will, a compassionate one would create only happiness, a purposeless one would not act; creation and dissolution are to be understood 'as today'.
arguments: ŚV sambandhākṣepaparihāra 42–68, 113.

sides.position: Things arise and perish gradually; people were always born of parents; no Īśvara moves atoms by will.
Īśvara creates the world from atoms at the beginning of each cycle and dissolves it at the end; his existence is inferred from the world as an effect.
Creation and dissolution recur in cosmic cycles (kalpas) under the Lord.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled; candidate readings listed.
candidate_readings: P1-level: Advaita reads creation-talk as empirical (vyāvahārika) — Mīmāṃsā accepts no such levels.
Kumārila's own Tantravārttika speaks of Manus in each kalpa, suggesting that cyclic time is not denied as such, only a total destruction and first creation; unresolved within his works.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Mīmāṃsakas reject any creator; Naiyāyikas and Purāṇic authors hold cyclic creation by the Lord.

notes: Related to dsp:isvara (U50).

question: Is the outcome of life decided by fate (daiva) or by human effort (pauruṣa)?

sides.position: Effort is everything; fate is nothing but one's own former effort and is overcome by present effort guided by scripture and the good; reliance on fate is delusion.
arguments: fate, unlike effort, is never perceived
'fate' is a name given to the fruit of one's own deeds
yesterday's misdeed is corrected by today's good conduct
beings became Indra, Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva by effort

sides.position: Everything is fixed by destiny (niyati); human effort has no power (as reported by Buddhist and Jain opponents).
arguments: beings are purified or defiled without cause or effort, ripened by destiny (reported)

sides.position: Both fate and effort are needed, as seed and field; effort is the field without which fate bears no fruit (the common epic and smṛti position).
arguments: the analogy of seed and field (recalled from the Mahābhārata's discussions of daiva and puruṣakāra)

reconciliation.explanation: The Yoga Vāsiṣṭha itself redescribes fate as past effort, so 'fate' and 'effort' name one causal process seen from past and present standpoints.
reconciliation.detail: Under P2 (causal standpoint) the epic 'both' position and the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha's 'effort only' position differ in wording more than in substance; the Ājīvika determinism, known only from opponents' reports, is not reconciled.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Ājīvika view as reported denies any efficacy to effort; the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha rejects the independent existence of fate.

candidate_readings: past-and-present effort (YV)
seed and field (epic)
strict destiny (Ājīvika, reported)

queries: local texts at the refs cited by dsp:daiva-or-paurusa
checks.note: Mokṣopāya side verified (2.4.8-18, 2.6.1-6, 2.8.1-5; beings became Viṣṇu and others by effort, 2.4.14, 2.7.31). The low-confidence epic side is confirmed at MBh CE 13.6.7-8, the seed-and-field analogy of the Vasiṣṭha-Brahmā dialogue. The Ājīvika report is at DN 2 (dn2:20.6, 'niyatisaṅgatibhāvapariṇatā').

notes: The epic side's reference is recalled with low confidence; the Ājīvika side is owned by U33.

question: Should the Goddess be worshipped in the right-hand (dakṣiṇa) mode, or is the left-hand/Kaula (vāma) mode with the five tattvas higher?

sides.position: The seven modes rise from Veda to Kaula; Vāma is higher than Dakṣiṇa and Kaula highest of all (Kulārṇava 2.7-8); in the Kula dharma enjoyment itself becomes yoga (2.23-24); worship of the primordial Śakti without the five tattvas is fruitless 'like seed on rock' (Mahānirvāṇa 5.22-24).
arguments: the bliss of Brahman latent in the body is made manifest in the Kula rite (Kulārṇava 5.79-80)
the Kula scripture is Vedic in essence (Kulārṇava 2.85)

sides.position: (Kālīvilāsa) In the Kali age all classes must worship in the paśu disposition, bathing thrice daily and eating no meat; the vīra and divya dispositions do not exist in this age (Kālīvilāsa 4.2-3).
arguments: each disposition belongs to its age (6.10-16)
the great exemplars (Rāma, the Sanakas) were perfected in the paśu disposition

sides.position: (Samaya Śrīvidyā, Lakṣmīdhara) The Kaula and 'mixed' modes are to be abandoned: the sixty-four tantras aim at worldly powers, deceive even their knowers and are far from the Veda; only the inner Samaya worship is Vedic.

reconciliation.explanation: The texts themselves tie the modes to the practitioner's disposition and eligibility (bhāva, adhikāra) and provide substitutes, so right- and left-hand worship are prescribed for different practitioners.
reconciliation.detail: The Mahānirvāṇa itself restricts the tattvas and substitutes the sweet triad for householders in the Kali age (6.14; 8.170-171); the Kulārṇava restricts Kula knowledge to the tested and eligible (2.30-36; 14.9-14) and condemns misuse (5.96-105). This covers the Kaula–Dakṣiṇa difference as one of stage; it does not cover the Kālīvilāsa's denial that the vīra disposition exists at all in this age, nor the Samaya rejection of Kaula as non-Vedic.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Kaula texts hold Kaula to be the highest for all who are eligible, not merely an option; the Kālīvilāsa denies the vīra and divya dispositions in the Kali age; Lakṣmīdhara's Samaya school rejects the Kaula way outright.

question: Was Dāmodaradeva a disciple of Śaṅkaradeva, or an independent founder?

sides.position: (Mahāpuruṣīyā account) Dāmodaradeva was initiated by Śaṅkaradeva and belongs within his dharma.
arguments: Carit-puthis of Śaṅkaradeva's line.

sides.position: (Dāmodarīyā account) Dāmodaradeva was an independent teacher whose line need not be subordinated to Śaṅkaradeva's.
arguments: The Dāmodarīyās' own hagiographies (not examined here).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: competing lineage histories.
candidate_readings: Historical: he received initiation but developed an independent institutional line.

question: Are precepts and practice needed once one has awakened?

sides.position: (Reported by its opponent Eisai) There are no precepts to keep and no practice to do: the mind is buddha from the beginning.
Eisai: the precepts are the foundation of Zen; one who does not keep them cannot practise Zen.
The Platform Sūtra: 'when the mind is level, what need to keep precepts?' — yet it gives formless precepts and repentance.

reconciliation.explanation: From the ultimate standpoint there is nothing to keep; at the conventional level precepts remain the foundation — the Platform Sūtra gives both.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Eisai treats the Daruma-school position as wrong view, not as a difference of level.

question: Should the devotee say 'I am He' (so'ham) or 'I am your servant' (dāsō'ham)?

sides.position: Not 'I am He' but 'I am your servant': the devotee's stance is humble service to Śiva and his devotees.
arguments: Basava's vacana.

sides.position: At the māheśvara stage the worshipper rejects total non-duality because Lord and servant must differ (10.37–43), but in śivayoga-samādhi the supreme self is contemplated as 'I am He' (12.21–24), at aikya the feeling 'I am Śiva' establishes oneness (14.5–7), and one who no longer thinks 'I am servant, Śiva master' stands in non-duality (14.37).

reconciliation.explanation: The SSM itself assigns servanthood to the stages of practice and 'I am He' to śivayoga and union (P4); the vacana speaks from the devotional standpoint, the SSM's aikya verses from the absolute (P2).
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Basava-centred readers hold dāsōhaṃ to be a permanent ethic of humility and service, not a stage to be outgrown, and hear 'sōhaṃ' in the vacana as the voice of ego.

question: Is birth settled only at death with the Buddha's welcome, or already in this life?

sides.position: Right mindfulness at death and Amida's welcoming descent are sought; the nenbutsu is continued so that the practitioner is welcomed.
Deathbed rites and assisted recitation secure right mindfulness; Daochuo's wax seal: the moment life ends is the moment of birth.
The welcome belongs to those of various practices; the person of shinjin is settled at the moment of shinjin and need not wait for the moment of death.

reconciliation.explanation: Shinran himself assigns the welcome at death to practitioners of the nineteenth vow and settlement in life to those of the eighteenth — a distinction by the practitioner's stage.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Jōdo-shū does not accept that its practitioners are of the nineteenth vow.

question: May a debater refute without holding a thesis of his own (vitaṇḍā)?

sides.position: Cavilling without a counter-thesis is a recognized but inferior form of debate, permitted only to protect truth; a caviller who states his purpose or meaning thereby adopts a thesis, and one who rejects all examples cannot refute anyone.
The Mādhyamika refutes the opponent's theses by consequences without advancing a thesis of his own: 'if I had a thesis the fault would be mine; since I have none, there is no fault' (Nāgārjuna).
arguments: Vigrahavyāvartanī v. 29 (as usually cited).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled.
candidate_readings: P6-upaya: the Madhyamaka's thesis-less refutation as a skilful means aimed at the opponent's clinging.
P1-level: absence of a thesis 'ultimately' while using conventional language.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Nyāya holds that speech always commits the speaker to a thesis; Madhyamaka denies holding one.

question: Can the categories and means of knowledge be coherently defined?

sides.position: No: every definition proposed by the Naiyāyikas (of valid cognition, of the means of knowledge, of the categories) fails on examination; the world of distinctions is indeterminable (Śrīharṣa's Khaṇḍanakhaṇḍakhādya), argued on the opponent's own rules.
arguments: Khaṇḍanakhaṇḍakhādya (as usually described).

sides.position: Yes: definitions can be made exact by specifying delimitors, relations and counterpositives; Gaṅgeśa's Tattvacintāmaṇi answers such objections.
arguments: Tattvacintāmaṇi (scholarly account of its motivation).

historical_debates.name: Śrīharṣa and Udayana
historical_debates.accounts: A popular tradition says Śrīharṣa wrote to avenge his father's defeat by Udayana (tradition's account; low confidence).
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: claimed by each side

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled.
candidate_readings: P1-level: Śrīharṣa's critique targets the ultimate status of distinctions, while Navya-Nyāya defends their empirical coherence.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Navya-Nyāya does not accept a merely empirical status for its categories.

question: Does dependent origination describe rebirth across three lives, or a process in present experience?

sides.position: The commentaries expound the twelve links across three lives: two past causes, eight present, two future — twenty modes and three links; the wheel has no maker or experiencer.
arguments: Visuddhimagga XVII's analysis.

sides.position: The whole chain arises in daily life at every unmindful contact; 'birth' is the birth of the ego; reading it only across lives makes it useless for practice.
arguments: The suttas' ordinary-language and Dhamma-language senses of 'birth'.

sides.position: The Vibhaṅga's Abhidhamma method already shows the links within one moment of consciousness, alongside the sutta method across lives.

historical_debates.name: Thai debate over Buddhadāsa's reading
historical_debates.accounts: Buddhadāsa's critique of the three-lives model drew conservative criticism; Payutto's Buddhadhamma presents both readings (recalled, low confidence).
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Both readings are taught

reconciliation.explanation: The canonical Abhidhamma itself gives both an across-lives and a single-moment exposition; each reading is a standpoint the tradition already contains.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Commentarial Theravāda insists that the across-lives reading, with literal rebirth, is not optional; Buddhadāsa rejected making it the primary meaning.

question: Where does the path of the gods lead: to the conditioned (kārya) Brahman or to the supreme Brahman (BS 4.3.7–16)?

sides.position: Bādari: to the conditioned Brahman, since movement to the all-pervading is impossible (Śaṅkara accepts this as siddhānta, with krama-mukti).
Jaimini: to the supreme Brahman, the primary meaning of the word.
Bādarāyaṇa: the guide leads those who do not meditate on symbols (Rāmānuja takes this as the final view: the path leads to the supreme).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: Advaita and Viśiṣṭādvaita take different sūtras as the conclusion.
candidate_readings: Advaita: the path serves saguṇa meditators and ends in krama-mukti; nirguṇa knowers do not travel.
Viśiṣṭādvaita: all released souls travel to the supreme Brahman.

question: Should forest dwelling, alms-food, rag robes, tree-root dwelling and abstention from fish and meat be compulsory for life?
