reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the Vedic schools agree the Veda is valid but disagree whether it has an author (Mīmāṃsā, Vedānta vs Nyāya), and the śramaṇa, Cārvāka and some bhakti and Sant voices deny or relativize its authority.
reconciliation.detail: Within the Vedic schools Vedānta takes a middle course — breathed out by Brahman yet not freely composed, re-manifest in each cycle with the same names and forms (BSBh 1.1.3; 1.3.28-30) — which accommodates the Nyāya concern (a source in the omniscient) and the Mīmāṃsā concern (no human author) but is accepted by neither. The Upaniṣads and the Gītā themselves relativize the Veda for the knower (MuU 1.1.4-5; BĀU 4.3.22; BhG 2.46).
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Mīmāṃsā rejects any author, the Lord included (ŚV sambandhākṣepaparihāra 66-68); Nyāya holds that validity requires a reliable speaker (NS 2.1.69); the Buddhists and Jains deny the Veda's claim over the supersensible; the Cārvākas deny it outright.

candidate_readings: P2-standpoint (Vedānta's middle): from the standpoint of its source the Veda issues from the omniscient; from the standpoint of its form and sequence it is never freely composed — rejected by Mīmāṃsā (no Lord) and by Nyāya (the Lord composes it anew).

P1-level / P4-stage (the Upaniṣads' and Gītā's own relativization): the Veda is the lower knowledge, of use until the flood of knowledge — for the knower 'the Vedas are no Vedas'; Mīmāṃsā does not accept a stage beyond the injunctions.

P7-arthavada: the Sants' and Tantras' disparagements of Veda-reciters read as censure of misuse, not of the Veda (Kabīr: 'do not say the Vedas are false') — the śramaṇa critics reject the Veda itself, not only its misuse.
notes: Cārvāka, Ajita and Bhūridatta sides and the Nyāya reply (NS 2.1.58-59) contributed by U33 are included verbatim.
alt_notes: U33 contribution; U50 owns the dispute and its reconciliation.

question: Is awakening sudden — an all-at-once seeing of the mind's nature — or gradual, reached by stages of cultivation and analysis; and after sudden awakening, is gradual cultivation still needed?

sides.position: Shenhui (Southern school): Bodhidharma's robe and the direct transmission passed to Huineng; Shenxiu's line is collateral, and its teaching — 'freezing the mind to enter samādhi, fixing the mind to view purity, activating the mind to illumine outside, concentrating the mind to realise within' — is gradual; the true teaching is sudden awakening.

The Platform Sūtra: the Dharma has no sudden or gradual; people's natures are sharp or dull — the deluded cultivate gradually, the awakened accord suddenly. Its gate takes no-thought as its tenet, no-form as its substance, non-abiding as its root; for one awakened to self-nature there is 'sudden awakening, sudden cultivation, without gradual steps', while Shenxiu's three trainings suit smaller faculties. Guishan: a beginner who suddenly awakens to principle in one thought still has beginningless habit energies to clear — that is cultivation.

The Northern school in its own words: the buddhas have a great expedient for entering the Way — with one thought of the pure mind one suddenly transcends to the buddha-ground; viewing the mind, if it is pure, is called the ground of the pure mind; awakening is the mind's substance free of thought, equal to space. (The Southern texts report Shenxiu's verse — the body the bodhi tree, the mind a bright mirror to be wiped — and his 'fix the mind, view stillness'.)

Moheyan (Chinese party at the Tibetan court): all beings are bound by deluded, discriminating thought; when thoughts arise, do not follow them — 'not thinking, not examining' — and the originally pure mind appears; the six perfections are included in this non-examining; entry into non-conceptuality is simultaneous, not by steps.

Kamalaśīla: there is no way other than correct analysis (bhūta-pratyavekṣā) to reach non-recollection and non-attention; mere absence of thought cannot cause non-conceptual wisdom, or one who has fainted would have it. Seeing by analysis that no dharma has arisen in the three times, the yogin enters non-conceptual wisdom; the path is gradual — calm abiding and insight, the perfections and the grounds.
The Kathāvatthu rejects the thesis that the truths are penetrated gradually (anupubbābhisamaya): each path penetrates the four truths at once.
The truths are realized in sixteen successive moments of acceptance and knowledge on the path of seeing — a graded, momentary sequence.

The Laṅkāvatāra: the stream of what is seen as one's own mind is purified gradually — as mangoes ripen — and also all at once — as a mirror shows all forms at once. The Avataṃsaka: at the first arousal of the mind one attains unsurpassed awakening. The Śūraṅgama: in principle awakening is sudden, in phenomena removal is gradual.

Zongmi: sudden and gradual, awakening and cultivation, seem opposed but accord and support one another; if one cultivates on the basis of awakening it is understanding-awakening, if one awakens through cultivation it is realization-awakening; 'first sudden awakening, then gradual cultivation' is like the sun rising at once while frost melts gradually. Over past lives there is only the gradual.

Jinul: though there are many gates, in essence they are two — sudden awakening and gradual cultivation; even the 'sudden awakening, sudden cultivation' of the highest faculties rests on gradual cultivation in past lives; the principle is awakened suddenly, habit energies are removed step by step.

(Recent) Seongcheol: the patriarchs' awakening is realization-awakening in which cultivation is also complete — sudden awakening, sudden cultivation; Jinul's formula describes only understanding-awakening.

Sakya Paṇḍita: the Mahāmudrā of his day and the 'Chinese Great Perfection' are essentially the same as the Hashang's teaching rejected in Tibet; true Mahāmudrā is the wisdom born of empowerment and the two stages.

The Ājñāsamyakpramāṇa: by the difference of persons' minds there are the gradual and the simultaneous; the medicine of one is the poison of the other — teach the simultaneous to one with the residue of former training, the gradual to beginners.

(An analogue in the Upaniṣadic yoga texts) The Varāha Upaniṣad distinguishes Śuka's path of the bird — immediate liberation through inquiry into the great sayings — from Vāmadeva's path of the ant — gradual liberation over births through yoga — and says both reach Brahman.

historical_debates.name: The Samye debate (bSam yas)
historical_debates.date: tradition: c. 792–794 CE under Khri srong lde btsan
historical_debates.accounts: Tibetan accounts (the Testament of Ba / sBa bzhed; later Bu ston and others) report a debate before the king in which the Indian party of Kamalaśīla, teaching the gradual path of the perfections, prevailed over the party of the Chinese master Moheyan, teaching sudden non-conceptuality, and the king ruled that Tibetans should follow Nāgārjuna's view and the gradual path. The Chinese Dunhuang document Dunwu dasheng zhengli jue (compiled by Wangxi) records Moheyan's answers to the Indian objections and presents his teaching as upheld. Kamalaśīla's third Bhāvanākrama argues against non-thinking as the way to non-conceptuality.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Tibetan tradition: Kamalaśīla prevailed and Moheyan left Tibet. Dunhuang Chinese account: Moheyan's teaching was vindicated. Nupchen's Samten Migdrön ranks the simultaneous above the gradual but below Mahāyoga and Atiyoga.
historical_debates.scholarly: Whether a single formal debate took place, or a series of written and oral exchanges, is disputed (scholarly account, labelled).

historical_debates.name: Shenhui's Huatai assembly
historical_debates.date: 732 CE (Kaiyuan 20), Dayun monastery at Huatai (tradition's account)
historical_debates.accounts: Putidamo nanzong ding shifei lun (record of Shenhui's challenge to the Northern school's claim to be the true line and to its 'gradual' teaching; the opponent named there is the Dharma master Chongyuan)
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Heze tradition: Huineng established as the Sixth Patriarch and the Southern teaching as sudden and orthodox; the Northern school's own texts (e.g. Dasheng wusheng fangbian men) present their teaching otherwise.

historical_debates.name: Kathāvatthu 2.9 (Anupubbābhisamayakathā)
historical_debates.date: tradition: the Third Council under Aśoka
historical_debates.accounts: Kathāvatthu 2.9 and commentary
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Theravāda: gradual penetration of the truths rejected; each path penetrates all four truths at once.

historical_debates.name: Seongcheol's critique of Jinul (recent)
historical_debates.accounts: Seonmun jeongno
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Contested within Korean Seon to the present.

reconciliation.explanation: Reconciled within Chan, Seon and the tantric Tengyur by their own principle that sudden and gradual lie in the practitioner's faculties, not in the Dharma (P4-stage), and by the reading 'principle is awakened suddenly, phenomena are removed gradually' (P1-level); the Samye question — whether non-conceptuality is reached by non-examining or only through analysis — remains not yet reconciled.
reconciliation.detail: Platform Sūtra 7.3 ('the Dharma has no sudden or gradual; people are sharp or dull'), Zongmi's ninth harmonisation and his sun-and-frost simile, Jinul's sudden awakening and gradual cultivation, the Ājñāsamyakpramāṇa's medicine-and-poison verse, and the Varāha Upaniṣad's bird and ant paths all assign the two to different kinds of practitioner or to different aspects (li and shi) of one path. The Śūraṅgama's 理則頓悟…事非頓除 is the P1 form.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Kamalaśīla and the Tibetan tradition after Samye reject non-examining as a path (Bhāvanākrama 3; Sakya Paṇḍita, Domsum Rabye 3); Shenhui rejects the Northern teaching as gradual and collateral; Seongcheol (recent) rejects gradual cultivation after awakening as mere understanding-awakening; the Kathāvatthu rejects gradual penetration of the truths that the Sarvāstivāda teaches.

candidate_readings: P4-stage for Samye: the simultaneous approach for those of sharp faculties or with former training, the gradual for beginners (Ājñāsamyakpramāṇa; Samten Migdrön's ranking) — rejected by Kamalaśīla ('no way other than correct analysis').
P6-upaya: 'not thinking, not examining' as a pointer to the ever-present mind rather than a technique — not accepted by the Tibetan critics, who read it as a method that leads to dullness.
Kathāvatthu vs Sarvāstivāda: 'at once' of the path-moment vs sixteen moments of the path of seeing — a question of how moments are counted within one path; neither school states this reconciliation.
notes: The Tibetan and Dunhuang accounts of Samye differ and are both recorded; neither is adopted.

question: Can a king be liberated while ruling — and may a woman renunciant test him? (MBh 12.308)

sides.position: Janaka Dharmadhvaja: taught by Pañcaśikha, he is liberated while ruling; a mendicant woman entering a king's mind by yoga commits an impropriety, mixing what should be kept apart.
arguments: Liberation is by knowledge, not by the outward renunciant's staff; his teacher Pañcaśikha.

sides.position: Sulabhā: one still attached to royal insignia, possessions and power is not free as he claims; analysing the body she shows it to be a composite that no one owns; she has done no wrong in entering his understanding by yoga.
arguments: His attachments contradict his claim of freedom (her own words: his claims are not borne out).
The body's constituents are shared; no fixed owner stands among them.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the dialogue records the challenge to the ruling king's claim of liberation and the objection to a woman renunciant's conduct.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: Janaka's claim concerns inner knowledge, Sulabhā's critique concerns conduct and attachment — both may hold from their standpoints
the dialogue's own weight falls on Sulabhā's reply, which the narrative gives the last word (to be confirmed in Phase D)
link to the general question whether women may renounce and teach (dsp:women-caste-liberation)

notes: Details of the argument summarized from memory apart from 12.308.7 and 12.308.16 (checked).

question: Is Viṣṇu or Śiva (or the Goddess) the supreme deity?

sides.position: Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa is supreme: Kṛṣṇa is Bhagavān himself; Brahmā and Śiva are his functions; Śambhu is the foremost Vaiṣṇava.
Śiva is supreme: he alone is niṣkala and worshipped in the liṅga; the column of fire whose ends Brahmā and Viṣṇu cannot find.
arguments: LiP 1.17

sides.position: The Goddess is supreme: she gives Viṣṇu, Brahmā and Śiva their bodies; beyond Hari and Hara.
arguments: DBhP 3

sides.position: Hari and Hara are one (the Kūrma's Īśvara Gītā; Gajendra's hymn reached Hari as all the gods).

reconciliation.explanation: Each Purāṇa exalts the worshipper's chosen deity (P3) with praise-language (P7); several Purāṇas themselves state the unity of the forms (VP 1.2.66; Kūrma), a standpoint reading (P2).
reconciliation.detail: The reconciliation claims only that the texts contain their own unity-passages; it does not claim the sectarian passages are non-literal for their communities.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Śrīvaiṣṇava, Mādhva and Gauḍīya authors hold Viṣṇu alone supreme and Śiva a jīva/devotee; Śaiva Siddhānta and Vīraśaiva authors hold Śiva alone supreme; Śāktas the Goddess.

queries: cited refs located in local e-texts
checks.note: All cited refs located (BhP 1.3.28, 8.3.30, 12.13.16; VP 1.2.66; ŚiP 1.5.10-28; LiP 1.17.33-34; DM MkP 81.65, 84.7; DBhP 3.3; KūP Uparibhāga 1-11 = Īśvara Gītā).

question: Should one refuse to affirm or deny anything about what lies beyond experience (the other world, fruit of deeds, the perfected one after death)?

sides.position: (As reported) Yes: to every such question, in each of its four forms, 'I do not say it is so, nor thus, nor otherwise, nor not so, nor not not so'; knowing is useless and ignorance better.
arguments: avoids false speech, grasping, and refutation (DN 1)
who knows whether the soul exists, and what use is knowing it? (Śīlāṅka)

sides.position: It is eel-wriggling born of fear or dullness; yet the Buddha himself sets some questions aside as not leading to the goal and declares what he knows beyond all views.
arguments: MN 76: the dull teacher is an unreliable holy life
DN 16: the Buddha sets aside Subhadda's question about the six

sides.position: The ignorant cannot settle their inquiry in ignorance or teach others; they are blind leading the blind.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the Ajñānika refuses to assert; Buddhist and Jain both assert, and both insist their own reticence (the undeclared points; the 'inexpressible' of the sevenfold predication) differs in kind from his.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: Sañjaya's refusal of four alternatives resembles the Jain 'avaktavya' and the later catuṣkoṭi — a resemblance noted by scholars (metadata only), rejected by both traditions.
P4-stage: the Buddha's setting-aside is tied to what benefits the hearer — not a general refusal.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Jains: syādvāda asserts under a standpoint, ajñāna asserts nothing. Buddhists: the Buddha knows and declares what is beyond views; the eel-wriggler knows nothing.

question: Can Mahāmudrā be introduced and realized apart from tantric empowerment — Gampopa's 'sūtra Mahāmudrā', the 'white self-sufficient remedy' — or is Mahāmudrā only the wisdom arising from empowerment and the two stages?

sides.position: Mahāmudrā is the nature of one's own mind; a realized guru can point it out through blessing to a ripe disciple, also on the basis of the sūtra teaching of buddha-nature, and recognizing it suffices ('the white self-sufficient remedy'); the tantric path of method is a second, complementary path, not the only door.
arguments: Indian precedent: Maitrīpa's non-mentation cycle and Sahajavajra's Mahāmudrā joined with the pāramitā path; Saraha's dohās (Gö Lotsāwa).
Tilopa: Mahāmudrā is not seen through the tenets of mantra, pāramitā or vinaya but by not engaging the mind (Gaṅgā Mahāmudrā).
Persons differ: the simultaneous way is medicine for those with prior training, poison for beginners, and vice versa (Ājñāsamyakpramāṇa) — the sudden recognition is not for all.
The Ratnagotravibhāga is the treatise of Mahāmudrā (tradition's report of Gampopa).

sides.position: Mahāmudrā, in the tantras, is the wisdom born from the empowerments and the completion stage; a 'Mahāmudrā' taught without them is not the Buddha's Mahāmudrā; the 'white self-sufficient remedy' is the teaching of the Chinese Hashang, refuted at Samye; the path needs the gradual accumulation of merit and wisdom.
arguments: The term mahāmudrā belongs to the mantra vehicle; outside it, 'Mahāmudrā' is a misnomer.
Present-day Mahāmudrā is in essence the Chinese Great Perfection.
A single remedy that dispenses with method contradicts the Mahāyāna union of method and wisdom (Sakya Paṇḍita's reasoning as reported).

sides.position: There is both a sūtra Mahāmudrā — the emptiness of mind realized by a mind that has established emptiness by reasoning — and a tantric Mahāmudrā — the clear light of great bliss; the Ganden (Gelug) Mahāmudrā tradition teaches both (First Panchen Lama).
arguments: recorded from memory; U47 owns the Gelug sources

sides.position: Sakya Paṇḍita: the Mahāmudrā taught by the Buddha is only the wisdom born of empowerment and the two stages; the present-day 'white self-sufficient remedy' taught without empowerment is the Chinese (Hwashang) Great Perfection under another name, and a fool's meditation on it leads to animal or formless rebirth or the śrāvaka cessation.
arguments: No such Mahāmudrā is found in the tantras.
It repeats the simultaneist teaching rejected at Samye.

sides.position: The Kagyu teach a Mahāmudrā of pointing out the nature of mind that can be introduced on the basis of sūtra (the Ratnagotravibhāga and Maitrīpa's teaching of non-attention), as Gampopa did; later Kagyu scholars answered Sakya Paṇḍita that his target was not their teaching.
arguments: Maitrīpa's amanasikāra teaching is Indian and not Chinese.
The Ratnagotravibhāga's buddha-nature supports a sūtra approach.

sides.position: The First Panchen Lama: Mahāmudrā has a sūtra approach (emptiness of mind as Nāgārjuna taught) and a mantra approach (clear light of great bliss); the various Mahāmudrā instructions converge in one intent.
arguments: The sūtra approach is meditation on emptiness taught by Nāgārjuna.

historical_debates.name: Sakya Paṇḍita's critique of Kagyu Mahāmudrā and the Kagyu replies
historical_debates.accounts: Sakya Paṇḍita's Discrimination of the Three Vows (and Clarifying the Sage's Intent) attack the 'white self-sufficient remedy' and Mahāmudrā without empowerment; Kagyu authors (Gö Lotsāwa, Pema Karpo, Dakpo Tashi Namgyal) answer by Indian precedent and by distinguishing approaches.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Kagyu: the critique misreads Gampopa's intent and ignores the Indian sūtra-Mahāmudrā precedent; Sakya: the criticism stands; Gelug: accepts a sūtra-level Mahāmudrā within its own Madhyamaka.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the sides disagree whether the guru's blessing without formal empowerment can be the cause of Mahāmudrā realization.
reconciliation.detail: Candidate readings are listed; none is accepted by both traditions.
candidate_readings: P4-stage: 'sūtra Mahāmudrā' is for persons of the simultaneous type with prior training (Ājñāsamyakpramāṇa 271a.3); Sakya objection — the Hashang made the same claim.

P1-level / terminological: the word names two things — the emptiness-luminosity of mind recognized through blessing, and the tantric wisdom of the fourth empowerment; if so the dispute is partly about the name; Sakya objection — the name is proper only to the tantric referent; Kagyu objection — the referent is one.
P6-upaya: blessing functions as an empowerment for the ripe disciple; Sakya objection — formal empowerment is required.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Sakya Paṇḍita rejects any Mahāmudrā outside the mantra vehicle; the Kagyu reject the identification of Gampopa's teaching with the Hashang's.

notes: Owned by U46; U47 supplies the Sakya and Gelug texts. Relates to dsp:sudden-or-gradual (the Samye background invoked by Sakya Paṇḍita). To be entered in RECONCILE_QUEUE.md by the orchestrator.
alt_notes: Sides contributed by U47 (Sakya Paṇḍita; Gelug Mahāmudrā); the Kagyu side is recorded only briefly and is owned by U46.

question: Is the gopīs' (and Rādhā's) love for Kṛṣṇa paramour love (parakīyā) or wedded love (svakīyā) in truth?

sides.position: Rūpa (Ujjvalanīlamaṇi) and Viśvanātha Cakravartin (Ānandacandrikā): paramour love in Vraja is the summit of amorous rasa, uniquely permitted there because Kṛṣṇa brought the gopīs down to taste rasa; Viśvanātha holds it eternal.
arguments: obstacles to union intensify love
the Vraja līlā is beyond worldly morality

sides.position: Jīva Gosvāmī: the gopīs are Kṛṣṇa's own internal potencies (Brahma Saṃhitā 5.37), hence svakīyā in truth; their apparent marriage to others is Yogamāyā's arrangement in the manifest play; the Gopālacampū ends with their marriage.
arguments: the Lord's śaktis are eternally his own
an eternal paramour relation would be improper

sides.position: Nimbārka tradition: Rādhā is Kṛṣṇa's eternal consort worshipped on his left (commonly described as svakīyā).

reconciliation.explanation: not yet reconciled: the Gauḍīya tradition itself records two positions, and the parakīyā party rejects Jīva's two-level resolution.
candidate_readings: Jīva's own two-level reading (svakīyā in the unmanifest truth, parakīyā in the manifest play) — analogous to P1-level; rejected by Viśvanātha
Viśvanātha's reading of Jīva's svakīyā passages as written at others' wish (Locanarocanī verse on intent) — a P6-upaya-type reading; rejected by svakīyā proponents
P3-path: different rasika temperaments — rejected by both parties as making a truth-claim a matter of taste
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Parakīyā proponents insist the paramour mood is eternal; svakīyā proponents that it is appearance only.

historical_debates.name: Bengal svakīyā–parakīyā debates
historical_debates.accounts: Gauḍīya accounts describe formal debates (e.g. at the court of the Nawab of Murshidabad, c. 1717–18, with Rādhāmohan Ṭhākur defending parakīyā)
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: the parakīyā side is said to have prevailed (low confidence; to verify)

historical_debates.name: Jaipur examinations under Sawai Jai Singh II
historical_debates.accounts: the Gauḍīyas' unmarried Rādhā beside Govindadeva and their sampradāya affiliation were questioned; Baladeva wrote the Govinda-bhāṣya
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Gauḍīya accounts say their position was vindicated

question: Is consciousness reflexively aware of itself (svasaṃvedana)?

sides.position: Every cognition is aware of itself as it is aware of its object; this self-awareness is the result of the means of knowledge, and memory of the experience proves it.
arguments: A cognition that is not itself known could not make its object known.
Memory of having seen presupposes self-awareness.

sides.position: Accepted conventionally: consciousness arises as the opposite of the inert, and its not being inert is its self-awareness; it is not an act of an agent on an object.
arguments: Self-awareness is the mark of consciousness (MAL 16–17).

sides.position: Rejected even conventionally: mind does not see mind, as a sword's edge does not cut itself; memory is explained without self-awareness.
arguments: The Buddha said mind does not see mind (BCA 9.17).
Memory does not require reflexive awareness (MA 6.73–75).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the Prāsaṅgika refuses self-awareness even at the conventional level, so P1-level alone does not bridge the positions.
candidate_readings: P1-level: self-awareness as conventional description only, never ultimately (Śāntarakṣita).
P2-standpoint: epistemological (pramāṇa) standpoint vs. soteriological analysis of the self.
P6-upaya: accepted as a device for refuting external objects, then discarded.

question: Is the validity of a cognition intrinsic (svataḥ) or extrinsic (parataḥ)?

sides.position: Validity is extrinsic: it is produced by an excellence in the causes of a cognition and is known not with the cognition itself but by inference — from the success of the activity it prompts or other marks; invalidity likewise comes from defects and is known extrinsically.
arguments: If validity were grasped together with a cognition, doubt about a cognition's validity could not arise, yet it does (Gaṅgeśa).
A means of knowledge is 'purposeful' because action based on it succeeds (NBh 1.1.1).

sides.position: Every cognition is valid by itself: validity arises from the very conditions that produce the cognition and is apprehended with it; invalidity is extrinsic, known from a defect in the causes or a later sublating cognition. A power not present in a thing by itself cannot be produced by another.
arguments: Extrinsic validation would need further validation without end.
The authorless Veda, having no author whose defects could vitiate it, is valid by itself.

sides.position: Both validity and invalidity are intrinsic — as reported in later doxography.
arguments: Reported, not argued here; e.g. in Mādhava's Sarvadarśanasaṅgraha (Jaimini chapter).

sides.position: Invalidity is intrinsic and validity extrinsic — as reported in the same doxographic scheme (Buddhist sources themselves are more differentiated).
arguments: Reported; to be checked against Śāntarakṣita's Tattvasaṅgraha.

sides.position: Validity is known through practical activity (vyavahāra) — whether the cognition leads to the object's efficacy (Dharmakīrti, PV Pramāṇasiddhi 5, conventional).
arguments: non-deception

sides.position: There is no single rule: some cognitions (self-awareness, inference, habituated perception, cognitions of efficacy) are valid by themselves, others only extrinsically (Śāntarakṣita and Kamalaśīla, as recalled).
arguments: Tattvasaṃgraha, Svataḥprāmāṇyaparīkṣā (recalled)

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the schools disagree about how validity is established.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: the Mīmāṃsaka thesis may describe the default acceptance of a cognition when no doubt has arisen, the Naiyāyika thesis the justification of validity once doubt arises.
P2-standpoint: both distinguish the arising (utpatti) from the ascertainment (jñapti) of validity; agreement may be possible on the first and not the second.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Both traditions insist on the difference: Mīmāṃsā needs intrinsic validity for an authorless Veda; Nyāya grounds the Veda's validity in its reliable author and cites doubt as proof that validity is not self-evident.

notes: The four-way doxographic schema (Sāṃkhya: both intrinsic; Nyāya: both extrinsic; Buddhists: invalidity intrinsic; Mīmāṃsā: validity intrinsic) is recalled from later doxography.
alt_notes: U41 contribution correcting the doxographic Buddhist side in U11's entry ('invalidity intrinsic, validity extrinsic').

question: How did the Śvetāmbara–Digambara division arise?

sides.position: During a twelve-year famine foreseen by Bhadrabāhu, the saṅgha went south with him and Candragupta; those who stayed in the north under Sthūlabhadra (or Rāmilla and Sthūlācārya) took up a half-cloth to beg in hard times and later a full white garment, becoming the Śvetāmbaras (at Valabhī, per Devasena, 136 years after Vikrama).
arguments: Hariṣeṇa's Bṛhatkathākośa (931)
Devasena's Darśanasāra (933)
Ratnanandi's Bhadrabāhucarita (15th c.)
The Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa inscriptions of the migration

sides.position: The Digambaras (Boṭikas) arose from Śivabhūti, who at Rathavīrapura, 609 years after the nirvāṇa, angered over a blanket, declared the naked Jinakalpa the only true renunciation; because his sister could not go naked, his followers denied liberation to women.
arguments: Jinabhadra's Viśeṣāvaśyaka Bhāṣya and the Āvaśyaka commentaries
The Pāṭaliputra council after the famine was held by the continuing community

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: each account makes the other the seceding group.
candidate_readings: Both narratives agree on a famine, a dispersal of the saṅgha and a dispute over clothing; they differ on who departed from the original practice

Scholarly account (labelled, not a reconciliation): a gradual differentiation over several centuries rather than a single event; the Mathurā inscriptions and images show a clothed tradition by the Kuṣāṇa period
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Each tradition regards its own account as history and the other's as polemic.

question: Is the soul the same as the body, or different from it?

sides.position: (As reported) The same: the soul is bounded by the skin; no soul can be drawn out and shown like a sword from its sheath; when the body is burnt nothing arises again.
arguments: burnt seeds do not sprout (Isibh. 20)
the sword-and-sheath challenge (Sūtr 2.1)

sides.position: Different: the soul is other than the body (Kesi to Paesi).
arguments: the fire-sticks simile

sides.position: Neither view is taught: 'soul is body' and 'soul is other than body' both make the holy life impossible; the Tathāgata teaches by the middle, dependent origination.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the materialist and the Jain affirm opposite answers; the Buddhist declines both.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: the Buddhist 'middle' is itself offered as avoiding two standpoints — but it does not accept either side's claim.
P5-neyartha: none recorded.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Each party insists on its own answer; the Buddhist texts count both others as extremes.

question: Can hymns in Tamil, composed by human poets — one of them born outside the brahmin class, one a woman — have the authority of the Veda?

sides.position: Yes: the Tiruvāymoḻi is the essence of the four Vedas in Tamil, the 'Tamil Upaniṣad', equal in authority to the Sanskrit and revealing its heart; Nammāḻvār's four works are the four Vedas, Tirumaṅkai's six the aṅgas; the Prabandham is recited in temples as Veda.
arguments: Ācārya Hṛdayam
Yāmuna's reverence for Nammāḻvār as 'first head of our clan'
the ubhaya-vedānta of the ācāryas
same purport as the Upaniṣads

sides.position: The Veda is authorless and eternal in its word–meaning relation; human compositions (smṛti) are authoritative only as inferring a Vedic source and are set aside where they conflict with it.
arguments: autpattika relation of word and meaning (MS 1.1.5)
smṛti authoritative only by inference of Veda (MS 1.3.2–3)

reconciliation.explanation: not yet reconciled
candidate_readings: P8-six-marks: the Prabandham shares the Upaniṣads' purport (opening and close, repetition, result) and so carries authority as to content without being apauruṣeya in form
P3-path: the Tamil Veda as the scripture of those (women, śūdras) barred from Sanskrit Veda-study — same goal by another door
Mīmāṃsā-style: the Prabandham as smṛti rooted in the Veda (authoritative by inference), which the Śrīvaiṣṇavas would accept only in part
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Śrīvaiṣṇava ācāryas (above all the Ācārya Hṛdayam) would reject any reading that makes the Tamil Veda secondary to the Sanskrit; Mīmāṃsā would reject calling any human composition 'Veda'.

notes: No Mīmāṃsaka text written against the Prabandham is recalled; the Mīmāṃsā side is stated from its general doctrine of scriptural authority, and the objections the Ācārya Hṛdayam answers (Tamil language, non-brahmin author) are the tradition's own report of them. Feeds dsp:status-of-veda (U50).

question: Is release won by Śiva's grace and worship, or by the Jina's path of self-discipline? (the Tamil Śaiva–Jain contests)

sides.position: Śiva alone saves by grace; the Jain monks' austerities, nakedness and denial of the Lord and the Veda are fruitless; the Lord's name, ash and temples protect the devotee.
arguments: The tenth verse of Campantar's patikams denounces Jains and Buddhists.
Appar's return from Jainism and survival of persecution by grace.

sides.position: Release is gained by right faith, knowledge and conduct, by one's own effort and austerity, without a creator's grace; non-violence is the highest dharma (position as held in Jain texts; in the Śaiva sources it is reported by opponents).
arguments: Reported here chiefly through Śaiva sources (reported by opponent).

historical_debates.name: The contest at Madurai
historical_debates.accounts: Periya Purāṇam and Tiruviḷaiyāṭal Purāṇam: Campantar cured the king's fever with sacred ash; in the fire ordeal his palm-leaf hymn did not burn, in the water ordeal it floated upstream on the Vaikai; the Jains, having wagered their lives, were impaled (the tradition's account; no Jain account of the event is known, and its historicity is doubted by scholars).
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Śaiva sources: victory of Śaivism and conversion of the king.

historical_debates.name: Appar's trials under the Pallava king
historical_debates.accounts: Lime-kiln, poison, elephant and the sea; he survived by singing Śiva's names and the king (identified with Mahendravarman I) became a Śaiva.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Śaiva sources: the king's conversion.

historical_debates.name: Māṇikkavācakar's debate with the Buddhists of Laṅkā
historical_debates.accounts: At Chidambaram he defeated Buddhist teachers and made the Laṅkan king's mute daughter speak (Tiruviḷaiyāṭal and later accounts).
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Śaiva sources: the Buddhists' defeat.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: a P3 reading (grace for the devotional temperament, self-discipline for the ascetic) is a candidate only.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Both the Tēvāram and Jain teaching deny that the other's path leads to release.

candidate_readings: P3-path: complementary paths for different temperaments
P4-stage: ethics shared, divergence in the ultimate

question: Are the Tamil hymns of the Āḻvārs (above all the Tiruvāymoḻi) Veda, equal in authority to the Sanskrit Upaniṣads?

sides.position: Yes: the Tiruvāymoḻi is the Tamil Upaniṣad (Dramiḍopaniṣad), the Veda's essence in Tamil; the teachers comment on both as one Vedānta (ubhaya-vedānta).
arguments: Nāthamuni received it from Nammāḻvār
Yāmuna's homage to Nammāḻvār
Deśika's Dramiḍopaniṣat works

sides.position: As the objection is reported in Śrīvaiṣṇava works: only the authorless Sanskrit Veda is śruti; a composition by a human author, in Tamil, by one not a brahmin, can at most be a devotional smṛti.
arguments: authorlessness (apauruṣeyatva) of the Veda

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled.
candidate_readings: P8-six-marks: the Tamil hymns share the Upaniṣads' purport
P3-path: the Tamil Veda as the devotional expression of the same truth
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Śrīvaiṣṇavas (especially the Teṅkalai) claim full equality, not a subordinate status.

notes: The opposing side is known here only as reported by Śrīvaiṣṇava authors (reported_by_opponent).

question: What does 'tat tvam asi' (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7) teach — identity of soul and Brahman, or something else?

sides.position: It teaches identity: 'that' (Brahman) and 'you' (the soul) are one consciousness; the words, stripped of their incompatible parts (by implication that drops part and keeps part), point to pure consciousness, as 'this is that Devadatta' identifies one person.
arguments: the ninefold repetition marks it as the Upaniṣad's purport
identity is the fruit that ends sorrow

sides.position: It teaches co-ordinate predication: both words denote Brahman — 'that' as the cause of the world, 'you' as having the individual soul as its body; the soul is a mode of Brahman, one with it as body with embodied self, yet distinct.
arguments: sāmānādhikaraṇya of two words with different grounds referring to one thing
the soul is Brahman's body (śarīra-śarīri-bhāva)

sides.position: It teaches difference: read 'sa ātmā atat tvam asi', 'you are not that', repeated nine times with examples that show difference (the bird tied to its post, honey from many trees, rivers in the sea); or 'aitadātmya' as being under the Lord's control and 'tat tvam asi' as dependence or likeness. Identity contradicts experience ('no one experiences I am omniscient, lord of all') and the conceit of it is the asuras' error.
arguments: experience contradicts identity
no scripture teaches non-difference; all teach difference
the examples illustrate difference
the Nyāyāmṛta refutes the 'impartite meaning' of the sentence

historical_debates.name: Akṣobhya Tīrtha and Vidyāraṇya at Mulbagal
historical_debates.accounts: The Mādhva tradition records a debate on 'tat tvam asi' between Akṣobhya Tīrtha and the Advaitin Vidyāraṇya, with Vedānta Deśika as arbiter, and a verse it ascribes to Deśika: that with the sword of 'tat tvam asi', which separates the Supreme from the soul, Akṣobhya cut down the great forest of Vidyāraṇya.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Mādhva tradition: Akṣobhya prevailed. The Advaita tradition does not accept this account, and the ascription of the verse to Vedānta Deśika is questioned outside the Mādhva tradition.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: all three sides read the same passage with the same exegetical rules and reach opposite purports.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Dvaita rejects any reading that makes difference a partial standpoint: the chapter teaches difference and only difference (VTN 1). Advaita holds identity is the sole purport; Viśiṣṭādvaita rejects both unqualified identity and Dvaita's separation of the soul from Brahman's body.

candidate_readings.reading: Identity (of consciousness), inseparability (of body and embodied) and difference (of substance) are each true from a standpoint.
Apply the six marks of purport to the chapter as a whole to decide its purport — a method all three sides accept but apply with opposite results.

notes: A focused exegetical dispute within U50's dsp:souls-one-or-distinct. The Advaita and Viśiṣṭādvaita sides are summarized from general knowledge; source refs for them are chapter-level.

question: Is the Tattvārthabhāṣya Umāsvāti's own commentary on the Tattvārthasūtra?

sides.position: Yes: the bhāṣya is Umāsvāti's own (svopajña); its praśasti names the author and his lineage; Siddhasenagaṇi and Haribhadra comment on it as such.
arguments: The closing praśasti.
Continuity of the Śvetāmbara commentarial tradition.

sides.position: No: the Digambaras follow the sūtra text fixed in the Sarvārthasiddhi and do not accept the bhāṣya as the author's.
arguments: The bhāṣya reflects Śvetāmbara readings (e.g. of the sūtra on the kevalin and on liberation of any sign).

candidate_readings: A historical question of authorship to which no reconciliation principle applies; record the tradition's accounts and the scholarly account separately (many scholars accept the bhāṣya as auto-commentary).

question: Are the ten practices of the Vajjian monks (including accepting gold and silver) allowable?

sides.position: (The Vajjian monks of Vesālī, as reported by the Theravāda Vinaya) Ten practices are allowable, among them carrying salt in a horn, eating when the shadow is two fingers past noon, and accepting gold and silver.
(Yasa, Revata, Sabbakāmī and the council of seven hundred) None of the ten points accords with the Dhamma and discipline.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the schools remember the Second Council and the first schism differently.
candidate_readings: See U38's dsp:cause-of-the-first-schism for the Mahāsāṅghika and Sarvāstivāda accounts.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Theravāda account presents the elders as upholding the original discipline.

notes: Attributing the Vajjian side to lin:mahasanghika follows the Theravāda chronicles; the Mahāsāṅghika sources give a different cause for the schism (U38).

question: Are saving life and giving to the unrestrained part of spiritual dharma?

sides.position: No: dharma is only what stops karmic inflow and fosters self-restraint; saving a being's bodily life by force or feeding those without vows is worldly (laukika) duty, not spiritual (lokottara) dharma, and may even support further harm.
arguments: The Jina's dharma lies in renunciation, not in preserving worldly life
Spiritual compassion leads a soul to restraint

sides.position: Yes: compassion (anukampā, dayā) that protects life and giving to the needy are religious merit and belong to dharma; the Jina's first teaching is non-harm and care for beings.
arguments: Compassion is a mark of right faith
Megha's compassion for the hare was praised by Mahāvīra

sides.position: Yes, with the Sthānakavāsīs: compassion and giving are meritorious.
arguments: As above

reconciliation.explanation: Bhikṣu's own distinction between worldly and supramundane dharma is a distinction of level: his opponents affirm compassion as merit (puṇya) and good conduct, which he does not forbid as social duty; he denies only that it is the spiritual dharma that stops karma.
reconciliation.detail: Both sides accept that merit (puṇya) differs from the shedding of karma (nirjarā) and that non-harm is the highest dharma.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Opponents deny that life-saving compassion is merely worldly; Terāpanthīs deny that it is spiritual dharma. The reconciliation claims only that they speak of different levels, not that either side accepts the other's classification.

historical_debates.name: Bhikṣu's separation from Raghunāth
historical_debates.accounts: Terāpanthī accounts; Sthānakavāsī counter-accounts.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Foundation of the Terāpanth.

question: Do the paths taught by the brahmins of the three Vedas lead to union with Brahmā?

sides.position: The various paths taught by the brahmins versed in the three Vedas — Addhariya, Tittiriya, Chandoka, Bavhārija — all lead to union with Brahmā, as many paths lead to one village.
arguments: Reported by the young brahmins Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja in DN 13.

sides.position: None of the brahmins or their teachers has seen Brahmā; their teaching is like a line of blind men; the path to companionship with Brahmā is the four divine abidings of a mind without hatred, like Brahmā's.
arguments: A line of blind men (DN 13.15).
One cannot call across the river Aciravatī to the far shore to come over (DN 13).
The brahmavihāras as the path (DN 13.76–81).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the Buddha denies that the three Vedas' paths lead to Brahmā and substitutes the brahmavihāras.
candidate_readings: P3-path: the Upaniṣadic and Buddhist traditions both teach companionship with Brahmā through inner qualities; the dispute concerns which path — but the Buddhist side treats the Brahmā world as within saṃsāra, not as liberation
reconciliation.tradition_objections: For the suttas union with Brahmā is at most a heavenly rebirth, not the goal; the Vedāntic traditions take brahmaloka or Brahman as final.

question: What happens in erroneous cognition (khyāti)?

sides.position: Misplaced apprehension (anyathākhyāti): a real property located elsewhere is apprehended as qualifying the thing before one (silver in mother-of-pearl).
arguments: Tarkasaṅgraha's definition of invalid experience; Gaṅgeśa.

sides.position: Non-apprehension (akhyāti): two cognitions — a perception and a memory — are not distinguished; no cognition is strictly erroneous.
arguments: As usually reported.

sides.position: Apprehension of the indeterminable (anirvacanīyakhyāti): the silver is neither real nor unreal but an appearance produced by ignorance.
arguments: As usually reported.

sides.position: Self-apprehension (ātmakhyāti): cognition's own form is taken as external.
arguments: As usually reported.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled.
candidate_readings: P1-level: Advaita's account presupposes levels of reality that Nyāya does not recognize; within the empirical level the accounts overlap in treating error as a presentation of what is not there.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Each school's theory of error encodes its ontology; Nyāya rejects the indeterminable and non-apprehension accounts explicitly.

notes: Positions other than Nyāya's are summarized at doxographic level; the owning units should supply texts.

question: Are the three vows (individual liberation, bodhisattva, mantra) one in essence, or distinct systems to be kept separately?

sides.position: The three vows are one in essence and differ only in aspect; they are kept together as one discipline, the higher including the lower (the 'single intent').
arguments: All the Buddha's teachings share a single intent (Gongchig).

sides.position: The three vows differ in how they are taken, kept and restored and must not be confused; Sakya Paṇḍita's Discrimination of the Three Vows sets out their distinct rules and criticizes teachings that blur them.
arguments: Confusing the systems leads to faulty practice (as reported).

historical_debates.name: The Gongchig and the Discrimination of the Three Vows
historical_debates.accounts: Sakya Paṇḍita's work is traditionally read as answering, among others, Drikung positions of the Gongchig (low confidence).
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: each tradition maintains its view

reconciliation.explanation: From the standpoint of essence (the motivation and view that the vows serve) they are one; from the standpoint of mode (ritual, rules, restoration) they are distinct — the Gongchig itself grants distinct aspects.
reconciliation.detail: The reconciliation claims only that the two statements answer different questions; it does not claim either school accepts the other's practice.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Sakya Paṇḍita's objection is precisely to the blurring of rules; Drikung holds its formulation already preserves the distinctions.

question: Are there three categories — soul, non-soul and 'no-soul'?

sides.position: The orthodox teaching (Śrīgupta): reality is soul and non-soul only; the twitching tail of a lizard is part of the soul's field, not a third kind.
arguments: Two-fold division of all substances
The test of the 'shop of the three worlds', where no 'no-soul' could be bought (as the tradition tells)

sides.position: Rohagupta (Ṣaḍulūka), as reported by the Jain tradition: there are three heaps — soul, non-soul and no-soul; he refused to recant and, the tradition says, went on to found the Vaiśeṣika system of six categories.
arguments: Having won a debate by asserting three categories, he held to them

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled; recorded as the Jain tradition reports it (the schismatic's own words are not preserved).
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: 'no-soul' as a name for a separated part of a living body considered as a mode, not a substance
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Jain tradition rejects the three categories as a denial of the Jina's word; the claim about Vaiśeṣika origins is the Jain account, not Vaiśeṣika's.

notes: Story details (the debate at Antarañjikā and the 'kutrikāpaṇa' test) recalled with low confidence.

question: Is the cause of birth the nenbutsu (with the three minds) or shinjin?

sides.position: The nenbutsu is the rightly determined act and cause of birth; the three minds accompany it.
Shinjin is the true cause (shinjin shōin); the nenbutsu is the expression of gratitude (shōmyō hōon).

historical_debates.name: The debate on shinjin in Hōnen's circle
historical_debates.accounts: Godenshō (the 'debate on shinjin' episode, Shinran's claim that his shinjin and Hōnen's were one)
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Shinshū: Hōnen affirmed that shinjin, being given by the Buddha, is the same in all.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled between the schools.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: from the practice side the nenbutsu, from the entrusting side shinjin — Hōnen's 'believe with one calling, practise with the whole life'
Shinran's own claim that the name and shinjin are inseparable (the name as the cause, shinjin as the condition, or the reverse)

question: Should one aspire to Maitreya's Tuṣita or to Amitābha's Sukhāvatī?

sides.position: (Aspirants to Tuṣita, as reported) Maitreya is the next buddha; being born in Tuṣita one hears him and descends with him; the ten goods suffice.
Tuṣita is in the desire realm, a place of retrogression and sensual attachment, without a vow to receive beings; in Sukhāvatī all are non-retrogressive and the vow and light embrace reciters.

historical_debates.name: Tuṣita vs Sukhāvatī comparisons
historical_debates.accounts: Anle ji; Jingtu shiyi lun; Xifang yaojue.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Pure Land: Sukhāvatī superior.

reconciliation.explanation: Both are Mahāyāna aspirations to be near a buddha; the Pure Land texts rank them by ease and non-retrogression rather than denying Tuṣita's value.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Daochuo and the Shiyi lun insist that the difference is 'great in substance', not merely of temperament.

notes: Xuanzang and Kuiji personally aspired to Tuṣita (recalled); the Xifang yaojue attributed to Kuiji nonetheless favours the West.

question: What divides the northern (Vaṭakalai) and southern (Teṅkalai) schools of Śrīvaiṣṇavism — the 'eighteen differences' (aṣṭādaśa-bheda)?

sides.position: Surrender is a means the soul performs once, with its limbs, and the occasion of the Lord's grace ('the young monkey clings'); Śrī is all-pervading, of the Lord's rank, and with him the means and goal; the Lord overlooks faults rather than relishing them; scriptural duties bind the surrendered as the Lord's command, and deliberate offences need expiation; kaivalya is not permanent.
arguments: scripture enjoins surrender as a means (Gītā 18.66, the Upaniṣads, Pāñcarātra)
a grace with no occasion would make the Lord partial
Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.8.17: as Viṣṇu is all-pervading, so is Śrī
the Catuḥślokī: even the Lord cannot measure Śrī's greatness

sides.position: The Lord alone is the means; surrender is not a means but acceptance fitting the soul's dependence ('the kitten is carried'); grace is causeless; Śrī is the mediator, not the means; the Lord relishes his devotees' faults; duties are kept as service and example, not as means or under threat; the teacher's regard saves; kaivalya is permanent.
arguments: the carama-śloka says 'me alone' and 'abandon all dharmas', including one's own surrender as means
the soul's nature is total dependence (pāratantrya)
the Lord's motherly love (vātsalya) relishes faults
the Tiruvāymoḻi and its commentaries

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the schools disagree on whether the soul's surrender is a means and on Śrī's rank; see the sub-disputes, some partially reconciled.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: the Teṅkalai speak from the divine standpoint (the Lord alone saves), the Vaṭakalai from the seeker's (surrender is what the seeker does)
P4-stage: the Teṅkalai stress what fits the utterly helpless; the Vaṭakalai what scripture enjoins on the qualified
shared ground: both hold the Lord as siddhopāya, surrender once, no last remembrance needed, release at the end of the body, eternal service
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Each school regards its points as doctrinal, not a matter of emphasis; neither accepts that the other's view is merely another standpoint.

historical_debates.name: Formation of the two schools
historical_debates.date: 13th–15th c. (doctrine); 17th–19th c. (separate institutions, marks and temple rights)
historical_debates.accounts: Each school traces its view to Rāmānuja through its own teacher-line; later polemical works list eighteen points of difference, whose exact list and author are not reconstructed here.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Both continue as living schools; disputes over temple rights (e.g. the forehead mark and invocations at Kāñcī) went to the courts in the colonial period (recalled; low confidence).

notes: The monkey/cat maxims are labels used in the dispute literature and later accounts, not arguments made in these terms by Deśika or Piḷḷai Lokācārya themselves (as far as recalled).

question: Which system — the Vedic Vaikhānasa or the tantric Pāñcarātra — is the proper basis of Viṣṇu temple worship, and must a Vaiṣṇava receive the branding initiation?

sides.position: The Vaikhānasa Sūtra, composed by Vikhanas (Nārāyaṇa/Brahmā), is the first and best of sūtras; its worship is wholly Vedic; Vaikhānasas are Vaiṣṇavas from the womb through the viṣṇubali rite and need no branding; its followers are the highest.
arguments: ten reasons (DHN)
Vedic mantras in every rite
prenatal consecration

sides.position: The Pāñcarātra is the Lord's own word, governing the chief self-manifest shrines (Śrīraṅgam, Melkote, Kāñcī), with the five sacraments as the mark of a Vaiṣṇava; only Veṅkaṭādri is excepted.
arguments: the three gems and their temple assignments
authority of the Lord's speech

historical_debates.name: Change of ritual system in Śrīvaiṣṇava temples
historical_debates.accounts: Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition credits Rāmānuja with establishing Pāñcarātra worship in some temples (e.g. Śrīraṅgam); the details are the tradition's account, not verified here.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Both systems continue in different temples (e.g. Vaikhānasa at Tirumala).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: each community holds its own system to be the better-founded.
candidate_readings: P3-path: two valid ritual paths to the same Viṣṇu, suited to hereditary Vedic eligibility (Vaikhānasa) and to initiatory eligibility (Pāñcarātra).
P4-stage: the Pādma's claim that Pāñcarātra eligibility comes 'at the end' of Mīmāṃsā learning is one side's framing of adhikāra.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Vaikhānasas reject being classed as tantric; Pāñcarātrins reject the view that their system is non-Vedic or lower.

notes: Bhāskararāya (Setubandha intro) quotes a verse saying the Lord taught the Pāñcarātra, Bhāgavata and Vaikhānasa for those fallen from the Veda — a third, Śākta view (recorded in notes only).

question: What is the self common to all men (vaiśvānara)?

sides.position: Each of the five householders and Uddālaka venerates one thing as the vaiśvānara self: the sky, the sun, the wind, space, water or the earth.
arguments: each view had its own fruit

sides.position: Aśvapati Kaikeya: each is only one part (head, eye, breath, trunk, bladder, feet); the vaiśvānara self is to be venerated as the whole, a span in size and beyond measure.
arguments: the whole eats food in all worlds, beings and selves (5.18.1)

historical_debates.name: Aśvapati instructs the six brahmins
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: The brahmins accept the king's teaching of the whole

reconciliation.explanation: The text itself treats each view as a true but partial aspect of one whole.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Aśvapati warns that each partial view alone would have brought harm; the parts are not sufficient in isolation.

checks.note: All 1 Upaniṣad refs cited in the entry are located in the prepared segments (ChU 5.11-18). It rests on 2 teaching(s) text-located in this sweep, and its wording matches those passages.

question: Is inference a valid means of knowledge?

sides.position: No (as reported by opponents): only perception is valid; pervasion cannot be established — perception cannot survey all cases, inference would presuppose inference, and testimony is itself inferential; Jayarāśi's scepticism extends even to perception.
arguments: Reported by opponents (Nyāya and doxographies); Jayarāśi's Tattvopaplavasiṃha is the extant sceptical text.

sides.position: Yes: the alleged deviations of marks (river swelling from damming etc.) involve different marks; the nāstika who uses an example has already given up his position, and one who refutes others must use inference.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled.
candidate_readings: P4-stage: some later Cārvākas (e.g. Purandara, as reported by Kamalaśīla) accepted inference about the perceptible world and rejected only inference to the supersensible — narrowing the disagreement to the unseen (adṛṣṭa, the other world, Īśvara).
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Nyāya treats the Cārvāka rejection as self-refuting; the Cārvāka side is known only through opponents.

notes: Cārvāka positions are opponents' reports (reported_by_opponent).

question: Is the Pāñcarātra a valid scripture, and does the Brahma Sūtra refute it?

sides.position: The Pāñcarātra is invalid: not rooted in the Veda, practised by Sātvatas/Bhāgavatas who are a low temple-serving class, classed by smṛti with heretical systems, and refuted by Bādarāyaṇa.
arguments: no pramāṇa establishes it
Manu names the Sātvata among degraded classes

sides.position: The worship of Vāsudeva by the five daily practices is acceptable, but the doctrine that the soul (Saṅkarṣaṇa) is born from Vāsudeva is refuted, and the system shows contradiction and opposition to the Veda (Śāṇḍilya turning to it after not finding the highest good in the Vedas).
arguments: an originated soul could not be liberated
an instrument (mind) cannot arise from an agent

sides.position: The Pāñcarātra is fully valid, spoken by the Lord; the Bhāgavatas are brahmins; the sūtras 42–43 state an objection that 44–45 answer, since the vyūhas are Brahman itself and the Pāñcarātra denies the origination of the soul.
arguments: Yāmuna's Āgamaprāmāṇya
Rāmānuja's Śrībhāṣya
Vedānta Deśika's Pāñcarātrarakṣā

historical_debates.name: Yāmuna's defence of the Pāñcarātra
historical_debates.accounts: Recorded as a treatise answering the objections point by point (Āgamaprāmāṇya).
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Śrīvaiṣṇavas hold the Pāñcarātra vindicated.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the sides read the same sūtras and the same vyūha doctrine differently.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: if the vyūhas are read as forms of the one Lord (Rāmānuja) rather than as the origination of souls (Śaṅkara's report), the Advaitin objection loses its object; Śaṅkara already accepts the worship portion.
P6-upaya: the tradition itself holds different scriptures suited to different devotees.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Advaitins hold that the Pāñcarātra does teach the soul's origination; Śrīvaiṣṇavas hold that Śaṅkara misreports it.

question: Is varṇa (and eligibility for austerity and teaching) fixed by birth, or made by conduct and qualities?

sides.position: Birth and nature: the varṇas' duties arise from their nature and one should not abandon the work born with one (BhG 18.41–48; 3.35); service is the śūdra's dharma (MBh 12.60.27–28; 5.40.26); Vidura, born of a śūdra womb, will not teach beyond this (5.41.5); in the Rāmāyaṇa the śūdra Śambūka's austerity is held to cause a child's death and Rāma kills him (7.74–76).

Conduct and qualities: one in whom truth, generosity, forbearance, good conduct, non-cruelty, restraint and compassion are seen is a brāhmaṇa (3.177.16); the whole world is of Brahman and came to varṇa by actions (12.181.10); the varṇas were made by guṇa and action (BhG 4.13); knowledge may be taken even from a śūdra (12.306.85); a meat-seller teaches a brāhmaṇa (3.198–206) and a merchant an ascetic (12.253–256); the wise see the same in a brāhmaṇa and a dog-eater (BhG 5.18); women, vaiśyas and śūdras too reach the highest goal (9.32).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the epics record both a birth-based order of duties and eligibility and repeated teachings that conduct and qualities make varṇa and that liberation is open to all.
candidate_readings: P1-level: sameness in the self and in the Lord (BhG 5.18; 9.29) at the ultimate level, varṇa duties at the conventional level
guṇa-karma reading of BhG 4.13 (varṇa by qualities and work) against the birth reading of the classical commentators, who take svabhāva as formed by past lives
bhakti reading: devotion and refuge open liberation to all regardless of birth (BhG 9.32; 18.66), while social duties remain
yuga reading (Rāmāyaṇa 7.74): eligibility for austerity differs by age of the world
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Dharmaśāstra and Mīmāṃsā hold birth-based eligibility (adhikāra) for Vedic rites and study; bhakti and reform readings reject birth as a bar to liberation; neither accepts the other's reading as the epics' meaning.

question: Are the four varṇas given by birth from the cosmic Person (RV 10.90.12)?

sides.position: The Puruṣa Sūkta: the brāhmaṇa was the Person's mouth, the rājanya his arms, the vaiśya his thighs, the śūdra born from his feet — the order of society belongs to the cosmic sacrifice.
arguments: The verse and its later use in the Dharmaśāstras as the charter of varṇa by birth.

sides.position: The Buddha mocks the brahmins' claim to be 'born from Brahmā's mouth' when they are seen born from women (Aggañña Sutta), and teaches that one is a brahmin not by birth but by action (Vāseṭṭha Sutta).
arguments: Birth from women is visible to all; conduct, not birth, makes the brahmin.
sides.note: The Pali texts report the brahmins' claim (their paraphrase of the Vedic view).

sides.position: Within the Vedic literature, the seers accepted Kavaṣa Ailūṣa, 'son of a slave woman', when the waters and gods showed him favour (Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 2.19, low confidence).
arguments: Divine favour overrides birth in this episode.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled.
candidate_readings: P1-level: the Puruṣa hymn speaks of the order of the manifest world (conventional), not of the worth of the self (the hymn also says the Person is all this).
P2-standpoint: cosmic-functional (the body of society) vs personal-ethical (conduct) standpoints.
The traditions themselves (Buddhist, and the bhakti and Siddha critics) reject any reading that keeps birth as the criterion; the Dharmaśāstras reject readings that drop it.

notes: Related to U50's dsp:women-caste-liberation (liberation) — this entry concerns the Saṃhitā verse and the origin of varṇa.

checks.note: RV 10.90.12 and AB 2.19 (Kavaṣa) located; DN 27 and Sn 3.9 are standard loci (not re-checked; SuttaCentral ids dn27, snp3.9).

question: Is the Yoga smṛti refuted by the Vedānta ('etena yogaḥ pratyuktaḥ', Brahma Sūtra 2.1.3)?

sides.position: Brahma Sūtra 2.1.3 declares that Yoga is refuted by the same reasoning as Sāṃkhya; Śaṅkara explains that Yoga is rejected where it teaches an independent pradhāna and a plurality of selves contrary to śruti, while yoga as a discipline and means is accepted.
arguments: Where smṛtis conflict with śruti on the cause of the world, śruti prevails.
sides.note: Summarized from memory; U13 owns these texts.

sides.position: Yoga holds a real prakṛti and many puruṣas (YS 2.17–25, 2.22); commentators answer that Vyāsa's Brahma Sūtras refuted the independence and reality claimed for pradhāna and a real difference of consciousness, not yoga as meditative cultivation, which the Gītā holds higher (Nārāyaṇatīrtha).
arguments: The yoga that is refuted is doctrinal, not practical.
Vijñānabhikṣu likewise harmonizes Yoga with Vedānta.

reconciliation.explanation: Both Śaṅkara's reading of BS 2.1.3 and the late Yoga commentators accept yoga as a path of practice while leaving the metaphysical disagreement standing (P3).
reconciliation.detail: Not reconciled: the reality and independence of pradhāna and the plurality of puruṣas.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Classical Yoga (Vyāsa, Vācaspati in his Yoga commentary) does not concede that its dualism is refuted; Advaita does not concede that it is true.

question: Is the killing prescribed in Vedic ritual an injury (hiṃsā) that brings demerit?

sides.position: No: the injury prescribed by the Veda is non-injury, for dharma shone forth from the Veda (MDh 5.44); animals were created for sacrifice.
arguments: the Veda is the sole authority on dharma

sides.position: Abstention is better: meat cannot be had without injury, killing does not lead to heaven (MDh 5.48); eating meat is natural activity, abstention bears great fruit (MDh 5.56).
arguments: the nature of meat
the fruit of nivṛtti

sides.position: The Vedic means are impure (aviśuddhi) because they involve killing; their fruit is also perishable (Sāṃkhyakārikā 2 as its commentators explain).
arguments: the general prohibition 'do not harm any being' is not cancelled by the special injunction

sides.position: Injury to living beings is never dharma, whether in ritual or not; the Śramaṇa traditions reject animal sacrifice.
arguments: non-injury as the highest dharma

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled.
candidate_readings: Mīmāṃsā: a specific injunction removes the general prohibition for its own case (no demerit)
Sāṃkhya: both apply — the rite yields its fruit and the killing its demerit
P4-stage reading of MDh 5.56: ritual meat is permitted at the level of pravṛtti, abstention is the higher nivṛtti
yuga-dharma: later authorities forbid animal (cow) sacrifice in the Kali age
Brāhmaṇa substitution: the sacrificial essence passed from animals into rice and barley (ŚB 1.2.3.6–9)

notes: Sāṃkhya and Jain sides summarized at text level from memory; their own units hold the verse-anchored teachings.

evidence: text:sources_raw/raw_etexts/mixed/gretil_devanAgarI/1_sanskr/6_sastra/4_dharma/smrti/manu-smrti_plain_text.md (GRETIL, Kullūka vulgate numbering; M = Medhātithi numbering)
checks.note: The Dharmaśāstra sides were found: MDh 5.39 ('yajñārthaṃ paśavaḥ sṛṣṭāḥ'), 5.44 ('yā vedavihitā hiṃsā … ahiṃsām eva tāṃ vidyāt'), 5.48 and 5.55–56. The Sāṃkhya side was found in Sāṃkhyakārikā 2 ('dṛṣṭavad ānuśravikaḥ sa hy aviśuddhikṣayātiśayayuktaḥ'), with the hiṃsā reading in its commentaries. The Jain side's citation, Ācārāṅga 1.4, belongs to another unit's text and was not checked here. That is why the result is partial.

question: Are the Śākta tantras Vedic and authoritative?

sides.position: Only the five Śubhāgamas, which teach the Vedic Samaya way, are fully authoritative for the twice-born; the sixty-four tantras aim at worldly powers, deceive even the learned, are far from the Vedic path and meant for others; the eight Candrakalā tantras are mixed.

Śrīvidyā is itself taught in śruti — the Tripurā, Bhāvanā, Kaula and Bahvṛca Upaniṣads — and the Gāyatrī is the Śrīvidyā; the Kalpasūtra calls itself a great Upaniṣad whose study makes one the performer of all sacrifices; the vidyā is hidden within all schools while the Veda is public. Bhāskararāya defends this with Mīmāṃsā reasoning.
Texts not accepted by those who know the three Vedas — including the Pāśupata and Pāñcarātra āgamas — have no authority as sources of dharma.

historical_debates.name: Bhāskararāya's defence of Śrīvidyā at Kāśī
historical_debates.accounts: The Bhāskaravilāsa is said to tell of his victories over Vedic critics (from memory; not checked).
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Victory for Bhāskararāya (the tradition's account).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the sides disagree about which texts are Vedic, not only about who may use them.
candidate_readings: P4-stage: all sides already distribute texts by eligibility (adhikāra); authority could be read as relative to the qualified practitioner.
P7-arthavāda: the Kalpasūtra's claim to be a great Upaniṣad and the Saundaryalaharī's disparagement of the sixty-four tantras may be praise and blame rather than doctrine.
P5-neyārtha: Lakṣmīdhara's classification may be provisional teaching for Vedic householders.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Mīmāṃsakas deny any non-Vedic source of dharma; Lakṣmīdhara denies the sixty-four tantras for the twice-born; Kaula Śrīvidyā denies that its tantras are outside the Veda.

question: Where the Visuddhimagga departs from the Vimuttimagga (e.g. on the number of temperaments), which account holds?

sides.position: Fourteen kinds of behaviour, including mixed types (Vimuttimagga, as reported).
Six temperaments in brief; counting combinations would be endless (Visuddhimagga, which cites the other view as 'some').

reconciliation.explanation: A difference of counting: both recognize the same basic temperaments and their mixtures.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Other points where Buddhaghosa rejects 'some' teachers' views remain to be collated (Dhammapāla's sub-commentary names Upatissa for several).

question: May one kill in battle as one's own dharma — and what of non-violence as the highest dharma?

sides.position: Arjuna: killing kinsmen is sin, destroys family dharma and leads to hell; it is better to be killed unresisting or to live by begging (BhG 1.31–47; 2.5).

Kṛṣṇa: the self neither slays nor is slain; for a kṣatriya nothing is better than a righteous war; acting without ego one does not slay even in slaying; the warriors are already slain by Time (BhG 2.18–38; 11.32–34; 18.17).
Non-violence is the highest dharma (MBh 1.11.12; 13.116; Tulādhāra 12.253–256; Vicakhnu 12.257); Satyavat argues against even capital punishment (12.259).
The meat-seller: no one lives without harming beings — even farmers and non-violent ascetics — so one's own inherited work done rightly is dharma (MBh 3.199).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the epic records both the kṣatriya's duty to fight a righteous war and non-violence as the highest dharma.
candidate_readings: P4-stage (adhikāra): the kṣatriya's duty belongs to his station; the ideal of non-violence to renunciants and ekāntins
P1-level: 'it neither slays nor is slain' (2.19) at the ultimate level, while the conventional duty of the warrior stands
action without ego and attachment does not bind (18.17)
allegorical reading of the battle as the inner struggle (Gandhi; recent) — rejected by the classical commentators, who read the war literally
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Jain and Buddhist traditions (outside this unit) reject killing as anyone's own dharma; the classical commentators reject the allegorical reading.

question: Does liṅga-initiation abolish caste and pollution distinctions among devotees?

sides.position: Yes: among liṅga-wearers there is no caste — Basava is the son of a cobbler's house and every devotee is 'ours'; the five pollutions do not apply; the intercaste marriage of Haraḷayya's son and Madhuvarasa's daughter enacted this.
arguments: Basava's vacanas.
The Kalyāṇa narrative.

sides.position: Devotion, not birth, makes the bhakta; the māheśvara drops jāti-dharmas opposed to the liṅga; at union brāhmaṇa and outcaste are alike and the realized are untouched by pollution — yet the practitioner eats with twice-born of his own jāti on the path, and the ordering of varṇa and āśrama is twofold (Śiva's and Brahmā's).
Varṇa and the rules of purity bind all; marriage across varṇa in the pratiloma direction is forbidden — the objection of the orthodox in the Kalyāṇa narrative (as reported in Vīraśaiva hagiography).
arguments: Dharmaśāstra rules of varṇa and marriage (general).

reconciliation.explanation: Within the SSM, commensality rules for practitioners (9.29) and equal vision for the realized (14.19–20) are assigned to different stages by the text itself (5.22–23); between the vacana strand, the SSM and dharmaśāstra orthodoxy the question is not yet reconciled.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Basava-centred readers reject any stage-based retention of caste among devotees; dharmaśāstra orthodoxy rejects the Vīraśaiva equality claim.

notes: Contributes the Vīraśaiva sides to the wider dsp:women-caste-liberation (owned by U50).

question: Did the Vīraśaiva/Liṅgāyata tradition begin with Basava and the śaraṇas of twelfth-century Kalyāṇa, or is it a beginningless Śaiva dharma renewed in every age by the five ācāryas?

sides.position: Vīraśaiva dharma is anādi: Śiva taught it in the later portion of the Āgamas and to the Goddess and Nandin; Reṇuka emerged from the Someśvara liṅga at Kollipāki and taught Agastya; the five ācāryas appear from liṅgas in every yuga and founded the five pīṭhas. Basava is a great devotee and reviver within this stream.
arguments: The SSM's own frame of transmission (1.28–31; 3.83–87; 4.1).
The Āgamas 'from Kāmika to Vātula' teach Vīraśaiva doctrine in their uttara-bhāga (5.14).
The Tattvapradīpikā already names the Pañcācārya lineage and links Siddharāma to Revaṇasiddha.

sides.position: The tradition was inaugurated by Basava with Allama Prabhu, Cennabasava, Akka Mahādēvi and the śaraṇas in Kalyāṇa; the vacanas are its founding scripture; the Pañcācārya narratives and the Sanskrit Āgamic framing come later.
arguments: The vacanas and the earliest hagiographies (Harihara's ragaḷes) centre on Basava and the śaraṇas.
The Śūnyasampādane presents Allama and Basava's Anubhava Maṇṭapa as the tradition's origin-scene.

reconciliation.explanation: not yet reconciled: the two accounts differ on a historical question (who began the tradition and when) to which the eight principles do not apply as a hermeneutic
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: the Pañcācārya account speaks from the standpoint of the dharma's eternal transmission, the śaraṇa account from that of its historical renewal — each side rejects this as diminishing its account.
Two streams — a Śaiva ācārya/maṭha stream and the Kalyāṇa devotional movement — later merged (a scholarly hypothesis, labeled; it also invokes a Kālāmukha background, see brw:kalamukha-to-virasaiva).
Basava as reviver of an older dharma (the Pañcācārya reading) — rejected by the śaraṇa strand.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Each strand holds its account as historical fact, not as a standpoint.

notes: Scholarly account (labeled): the śaraṇa movement is datable to the 12th c.; the Sanskrit Pañcācārya literature is attested later and its dating is debated; some scholars also point to pre-Basava Kannada Śaiva devotees (Dēvara Dāsimayya, Ēkānta Rāmayya) and to Kālāmukha antecedents.

question: Is Śiva to be worshipped in temples and installed images (the fixed), or in the personal liṅga and the living devotee (the moving)?

sides.position: Installed liṅgas in temples are proper seats of Śiva's worship for the community (temple worship as taught in the Āgamas).
arguments: Āgamic temple ritual (general; U08/U18 supply texts).

sides.position: The fixed shall perish, the moving endures; the body is the temple; to feed the stone snake and drive off the living devotee is hypocrisy.
arguments: Basava's vacanas.

sides.position: Graded: palm-worship of the iṣṭaliṅga excels pedestal worship; the inner liṅga excels stone liṅgas and clinging only to the outer is delusion; yet the nirmālya of fixed liṅgas is not to be used and fixed liṅgas are to be protected.

reconciliation.explanation: Within the Vīraśaiva texts the forms of worship are graded by stage (outer liṅga for all, inner for the advanced; 6.48; 15.44); vis-à-vis Āgamic temple Śaivism the question is not yet reconciled.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The vacana strand does not treat temple worship as a lower stage but rejects it; temple Śaivism does not accept the iṣṭaliṅga as replacing public worship.

question: What authority do the Veda and the Āgamas have for Vīraśaivas?

sides.position: The Veda is the chief authority; the Śaiva Siddhānta Āgama is 'made of the Veda', one with it in meaning and as authoritative; the Vīraśaiva doctrine is taught in the Āgamas' later portion and agrees with Veda and Vedānta — though sacrifices and austerities without Śiva-devotion are fruitless and not worth a fraction of liṅga-worship.
arguments: SSM 5.3–14 on authority.
SSM 6.58–61 reads the Ṛgveda as enjoining liṅga-wearing.
SSM 8.36–43; 11.48–49; 15.30–36 subordinate sacrifice to devotion.

sides.position: Scripture is to be tested by experience: Basava will put the Veda to the touchstone, fetter the śāstras and cut the nose of the Āgamas; the śaraṇas' vacanas and anubhava are the authority.
arguments: Basava's vacana 'Vēdakke oregalla kaṭṭuve'.
Basava's refusal of the sacred-thread rite (hagiography).

sides.position: The Ārādhyas wear the liṅga and worship Śiva exclusively while keeping the sacred thread and Vedic rites.
arguments: Tradition-account of the Ārādhya community (low confidence).

reconciliation.explanation: Within the SSM, reverence for the Veda and the subordination of Vedic rites to liṅga-worship are reconciled by stage (5.22–23; 9.39–40; 15.30–36); between the SSM and the vacanas the question is not yet reconciled.
reconciliation.detail: Candidate for the inter-strand question: P7-arthavada (the vacana's 'touchstone' as praise of devotion rather than doctrinal rejection) — a reading the Basava-centred strand rejects.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Basava-centred readers hold the vacana's rejection of Vedic authority to be meant literally; the Ārādhya and Pañcācārya positions hold Vedic authority non-negotiable.

question: Is the self the body (as seen in its reflection)?

sides.position: Virocana, for the asuras: the bodily self alone is to be worshipped and served here; by serving it one wins both worlds — hence the dead are adorned with food, clothes and ornaments.
arguments: the person seen in the eye and in water is the adorned body (ChU 8.8.1-3)

sides.position: Prajāpati's final teaching as received by Indra: the body is mortal, the base of the immortal bodiless self, which is free from evil, old age, death and sorrow and appears in its own form in the highest light.
arguments: the reflection perishes with the body (8.9.1)
the bodiless is untouched by pleasure and pain (8.12.1)

historical_debates.name: Indra and Virocana with Prajāpati
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Virocana's view is 'the upaniṣad of the asuras'; Indra reaches the self

reconciliation.explanation: The body-self is the first of four successive teachings given to a student; Virocana stopped at the first stage, Indra went on to the last.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: ChU 8.8.4 says those who hold this doctrine will perish; the P4 reading claims only that it is a provisional stage, never a valid final view.

checks.note: All 3 Upaniṣad refs cited in the entry are located in the prepared segments (ChU 8.8.1-3; ChU 8.7-12; ChU 8.8.4). It rests on 5 teaching(s) text-located in this sweep, and its wording matches those passages.

question: The rivalry of the priestly houses of Viśvāmitra and Vasiṣṭha

sides.position: Viśvāmitra's house: Viśvāmitra is priest of the Bharatas and of Sudās (RV 3.33, 3.53); the closing imprecations of 3.53 are traditionally taken as aimed at Vasiṣṭha, and Vasiṣṭha's descendants do not recite them.
arguments: The Bharatas' crossing of the rivers by Viśvāmitra's word; the imprecation verses.

sides.position: Vasiṣṭha's house: Vasiṣṭha is Sudās's priest in the Battle of the Ten Kings (7.18, 7.33) and swears 'may I die today if I am a sorcerer', against one who falsely called him so (7.104.15).
arguments: Victory of Sudās through the Vasiṣṭhas' prayers.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: a rivalry of lineages, remembered differently by each house and by the epics.
candidate_readings: The epic account (Rāmāyaṇa, Bāla-kāṇḍa) resolves it by Viśvāmitra's tapas and Vasiṣṭha's final acknowledgement of him as brahmarṣi — a P4-stage reading (change of standing through attainment).
