The two houses served one king at different times (a historical, non-doctrinal reading).
The attributions of the imprecations and of the sorcery charge are commentarial and may not concern Vasiṣṭha at all.

notes: The traditional attribution of 3.53.21–24 and 7.104 to this rivalry is recalled from commentarial literature with moderate-low confidence.

checks.note: The low-confidence traditional attributions are confirmed in Sāyaṇa: on 3.53.21 the four verses are 'vasiṣṭhadveṣiṇyaḥ', Viśvāmitra cursed Vasiṣṭha with them and 'the Vasiṣṭhas do not listen to them'; on 7.104.15 the verse is Vasiṣṭha's oath against being called a rākṣasa.

question: Is the Vrātya an exalted cosmic figure or an outsider to be brought into the Vedic fold?

sides.position: The Atharvaveda's Vrātya book exalts the Vrātya: he stirs Prajāpati, becomes Mahādeva and Īśāna, and a king should honour the knowing Vrātya above himself.
arguments: AVŚ 15 throughout.

sides.position: The Sāmaveda Brāhmaṇa tradition prescribes the vrātyastoma rites by which vrātyas — people living outside Vedic rules — are admitted to Vedic society.
arguments: Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa 17.1–4 (reference from memory).
sides.note: Locus recalled from memory (moderate-low); U02 owns the Brāhmaṇas.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: the Atharvaveda speaks of an ideal, cosmic Vrātya 'who knows thus'; the Brāhmaṇa of actual vrātya groups.
P7-arthavāda: the exaltation of the Vrātya is praise of the knower, not a description of vrātya groups.
Commentators (e.g. Sāyaṇa) take the Vrātya of AVŚ 15 to be a learned, revered figure or the Supreme (recalled, low confidence).

notes: Scholarly hypotheses linking the vrātyas to early Rudra-worshipping or ascetic groups are metadata only (see brw:vratya-and-saiva-ascetics).

checks.note: Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa 17.1–4 vrātyastomas located (hīnā vā ete hīyante ye vrātyāṃ pravasanti …) — the locus from memory is exact. Sāyaṇa on AVŚ 15: introduces vrātya as one without upanayana, yet on 15.1.1 calls the Vrātya 'vidvattama, mahādhikāra, puṇyaśīla, viśvasaṃmānya' — confirming 'a learned, revered figure'; the 'or the Supreme' alternative not seen.

question: What sees — the eye, consciousness, or neither?

sides.position: The eye sees, as the support of consciousness, since forms behind a wall are not seen.
Neither: visual consciousness arises from eye and form; 'the eye sees' and 'consciousness cognizes' are conventions over a mere set of dharmas without activity.

reconciliation.explanation: The Sautrāntika itself accepts 'the eye sees' as a valid convention; disagreement remains on whether it is also true in the ultimate sense.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Vaibhāṣika holds that the eye really sees and would reject treating its thesis as merely conventional.

question: May one renounce directly, at any stage of life, or only after passing through the householder's duties?

sides.position: Renounce on the very day dispassion arises, from studentship, household or forest; true renunciation is inner union of jīva and Self.
arguments: Jābāla 4: 'yad ahar eva virajet tad ahar eva pravrajet'
Nāradaparivrājaka 3: renunciation without dispassion leads to a fall; the self-controlled may renounce unmarried
Maitreya 2.17: renunciation is not abandoning rites but union with the Self

sides.position: Renunciation comes in due order, after the three debts (study, offspring, sacrifice) are paid; seeking liberation before paying them leads downward.
arguments: Manusmṛti 6.35–37 on the three debts
the Kuṇḍikā and Kaṭharudra themselves describe renunciation after studentship, marriage and sacrifices

historical_debates.name: Brahmasūtra 3.4.18–20: are the other stages of life enjoined?
historical_debates.accounts: The sūtras report Jaimini's view that scripture only mentions the other stages without enjoining them and Bādarāyaṇa's that they are to be practised; Śaṅkara, commenting, cites the Jābāla's rule on renouncing directly.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Advaita: renunciation is enjoined and may be taken directly.

reconciliation.explanation: The texts tie the timing to the renouncer's qualification: in due order for most, at once for one of intense dispassion; and the Maitreya distinguishes outer ritual renunciation from inner renunciation.
reconciliation.detail: The Nāradaparivrājaka itself says that renouncing without dispassion causes a fall, which grounds the adhikāra reading (P4); the Maitreya's definition places true renunciation on the level of knowledge (P1).
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Ritualists (Mīmāṃsā) hold that lifelong Vedic duties cannot be set aside; the Jābāla's partisans hold that dispassion alone decides, whatever one's stage.

checks.note: The external refs were checked locally: Manusmṛti 6.35-37 on the three debts (SARIT e-text), and Brahmasūtra 3.4.18-20 with Śaṅkara citing the Jābāla at 3.4.20 (GRETIL). All 5 teachings it rests on exist and were located in the e-text.

question: Which 'Bhāgavata' is the Mahāpurāṇa of the lists - the Śrīmad (Viṣṇu) Bhāgavata or the Devī Bhāgavata?

sides.position: The Śrīmad Bhāgavata is the Mahāpurāṇa: it begins with the Gāyatrī-marked verse, contains Vṛtra's slaying and has 18,000 verses (Matsya 53.20-22), calls itself the essence of all Vedānta and the fruit of the Veda-tree.
arguments: the Matsya definition fits it
its own verse count (12.13.9)
its opening 'dhīmahi' evokes the Gāyatrī

sides.position: The Devī Bhāgavata is the Mahāpurāṇa 'Bhāgavata'; the Viṣṇu Bhāgavata is an Upapurāṇa (some polemicists alleged it was composed by Vopadeva).
arguments: it too has 18,000 verses and treats the Gāyatrī and the slaying of Vṛtra
the Devī Bhāgavata's own list of Purāṇas

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: both sides apply the same Matsya definition to different texts; no principle decides identity of a title.
candidate_readings: P3-path: each is the 'Bhāgavata' for its community of worshippers (Vaiṣṇava, Śākta) - both traditions would reject this as evading the question.
The lists' 'Bhāgavata' predates both extant texts and the title was later claimed by each.
Scholarly metadata: modern scholars date both later than the lists' earliest layers.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Vaiṣṇava commentators insist on the Śrīmad Bhāgavata alone; Śākta authors on the Devī Bhāgavata.

question: Which deity is the supreme Brahman — Śiva, Viṣṇu/Nārāyaṇa, or the Goddess?

sides.position: Śiva/Rudra is supreme: he alone was in the beginning; as Śarabha he subdued Nṛsiṃha; Śiva alone is to be meditated on.
arguments: Atharvaśiras 1
Śarabha
Atharvaśikhā

sides.position: Nārāyaṇa is supreme: Brahmā and Rudra are born from him; Nārāyaṇa alone existed in the beginning.
arguments: Nārāyaṇa 1
Mahā 1

sides.position: The Goddess is supreme: she alone was in the beginning and gave birth to Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Rudra.
arguments: Bahvṛca 1–3
Devī 1–2

reconciliation.explanation: The identity Upaniṣads read the names as one reality (Viṣṇu the heart of Śiva, Śiva of Viṣṇu), and each sectarian text's supremacy claim can be read as praise of the chosen deity.
reconciliation.detail: Skanda 8–9, Rudrahṛdaya 1–5 and Kaivalya 8–10 identify the gods; the chosen-deity principle (P3) and the arthavāda reading of exaltation over rivals (P7) account for the sectarian texts.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Sectarian theologians deny that their supremacy claims are mere praise; the Śarabha's subjugation of Nṛsiṃha is rejected by Vaiṣṇavas, and Śaiva authors reject the Mahā's account of Śiva's birth from Nārāyaṇa.

question: Which part of the embryo forms first?

sides.position: The head, seat of the senses (Kumāraśiras Bharadvāja); the heart, seat of consciousness (Kāṅkāyana); the navel, where nourishment enters (Bhadrakāpya); the rectum, seat of wind (Bhadraśaunaka); hands and feet (Baḍiśa); the senses (Janaka of Videha); unknowable (Mārīci Kaśyapa).
Dhanvantari, approved by Ātreya: all limbs form at once, since all things are mutually bound.

reconciliation.explanation: Each sage names the seat of what he takes as primary; Ātreya adopts simultaneity because the parts are interdependent.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The single-first views are rejected, not merged, by Ātreya.

notes: Suśruta has a parallel list of opinions (Śā 3) — recalled, not checked.

question: Which aim of life is foremost — dharma, artha, kāma, their combination, or liberation?

sides.position: The combination, with dharma weightiest: the settled view is that the good is the triad (MDh 2.224); dharmaśāstra prevails over arthaśāstra (YS 2.21); self-knowledge leads to the supreme good (MDh 12.85).
arguments: dharma as the root of the others' legitimacy
liberation after the debts are paid

sides.position: Artha is foremost, for dharma and kāma are rooted in artha (Kauṭilya).
arguments: the world's livelihood depends on wealth

sides.position: The three are to be pursued in balance over the stages of life, each earlier weightier, artha first for a king; kāma needs its own śāstra.
arguments: the allotment of aims to ages of life

sides.position: Lokāyatikas (as reported by Vātsyāyana): dharma should not be practised, its fruit being future and doubtful — better a pigeon today than a peacock tomorrow.
arguments: uncertainty of unseen fruit

reconciliation.explanation: The texts themselves distribute the aims over the stages of life and over active and quiescent paths (Kāmasūtra 1.2.2–4; MDh 12.88–90).
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Kauṭilya still holds artha foremost; the Lokāyata view (known only as reported) rejects dharma altogether; for Manu the triad is subordinate to self-knowledge.

historical_debates.accounts: In the Śāntiparvan (MBh 12.161, as usually cited) Vidura, Arjuna, Nakula–Sahadeva and Bhīma each argue for an aim and Yudhiṣṭhira points beyond them.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: recorded in the Mahābhārata (U05); details from memory, to be checked

question: Which turning of the dharma-wheel is of definitive meaning (nītārtha): the teaching of emptiness (second) or the 'well-distinguished' teaching of the three natures and of buddha-nature (third)?

sides.position: The sūtras teaching emptiness, the signless, no self and no being are definitive; those teaching self, a being, or a truly existent base are provisional (Akṣayamati); the tathāgatagarbha is emptiness taught with an intention (Laṅkāvatāra).
arguments: The Akṣayamatinirdeśa's criterion of nītārtha.
The Laṅkāvatāra's own gloss of the tathāgatagarbha as emptiness taught to remove fear of no-self.
Candrakīrti (Madhyamakāvatāra 6.94-95, U40) reads the Laṅkāvatāra so.

sides.position: The first two turnings are surpassable and provisional; the third, which distinguishes the three natures and three naturelessnesses, is unsurpassed and definitive (Saṃdhinirmocana ch. 7).
arguments: The Saṃdhinirmocana's own statement about the three turnings.

sides.position: The third turning's tathāgatagarbha sūtras and the Ratnagotravibhāga are definitive: the ultimate (dharmakāya, buddha-nature) is empty of what is other than it — the adventitious stains — and not empty of its own qualities (shentong).
arguments: Śrīmālā ch. 9 and RGV 1.154-155: empty of stains, not empty of qualities.
Dolpopa's Mountain Doctrine (U48).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: P5 is the Buddhist traditions' own hermeneutic and all sides accept it, but it names the distinction without settling its application.
candidate_readings: Rimé reading (Jamgön Kongtrul, U48): the second turning is definitive about the emptiness of the relative, the third about the ultimate — both definitive in their own sphere.
Stage reading (P4): the turnings addressed disciples of different capacities (Saṃdhinirmocana itself).
Madhyamaka reading: third-turning statements are provisional (P5) but purposeful (RGV 1.156-157, P6).
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Gelug rejects the shentong reading; Jonang rejects the reading of the third turning as provisional.

question: What makes one a brāhmaṇa — birth, body, learning, action, or realization of the Self?

sides.position: Not jīva, body, birth, learning, action or dharmic deeds; the brāhmaṇa is one who has realized the non-dual Self and is free of faults; caste belongs to convention.
arguments: Vajrasūci: seers born of deer, jackal, anthill, fisherwoman
Nirālamba: caste is not of skin, blood, flesh or bone; imagined for convention

sides.position: Varṇa is by birth, with conduct and rites determining standing within it.
arguments: the Vajrasūci's own opening states the received view: 'of the four castes the brāhmaṇa is chief, say the Vedas and smṛtis'

reconciliation.explanation: The Nirālamba itself places caste in convention (vyavahāra) and the true brāhmaṇa at the level of realized truth, so both can hold on different levels.
reconciliation.detail: Read by levels of truth, birth-caste operates in conventional social and ritual life, while the Vajrasūci defines the brāhmaṇa by realization.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Dharmaśāstra authors would not accept that varṇa is merely imagined; the Vajrasūci claims its definition is the intent of all scripture, not merely a higher level.

question: Who may learn and recite the Veda?

sides.position: The recitation lineages transmit the Veda to the initiated (upanayana) twice-born; the Purāṇa says the triple Veda is not for the hearing of women, śūdras and lapsed twice-born, for whom Vyāsa composed the Mahābhārata (Bhāgavata 1.4.25); the Brahma Sūtra denies śūdras the right to Vedic study (1.3.34–38).
arguments: Eligibility (adhikāra) follows initiation.

sides.position: The Saṃhitās themselves record women seers (ṛṣikās) of hymns, a maiden's brahmacarya (AVŚ 11.5.18), a seer 'son of a slave woman' accepted by the gods (AB 2.19), and a verse speaking auspicious speech to brahmin, rājanya, śūdra, ārya, one's own and the stranger (VS 26.2).
arguments: The seers' own record.

sides.position: Dayānanda (recent): Vedic study and initiation are open to all, women and men of every birth, citing VS 26.2.
sides.note: Recent (post-1800).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled.
candidate_readings: P4-stage (adhikāra): the tradition's own frame — different texts and practices (Veda; epic and Purāṇa; the divine name) for different eligibilities — which the restricted parties and later reformers reject when eligibility is by birth.
Historical: women's Vedic study (brahmavādinīs) is attested in the Saṃhitās and early sūtras and was later restricted.
VS 26.2 read narrowly (addressing all with auspicious words at the rite) or broadly (teaching the Veda to all).

notes: Related to U50's dsp:women-caste-liberation.

question: Who is eligible to renounce?

sides.position: Restrictive: lists of the ineligible (the impotent, fallen, deformed, heretics, the unlearned and others); the ineligible may renounce only when at the point of death.
arguments: Nāradaparivrājaka 3.1–11
Sannyāsa 2.1–5

sides.position: Open: anyone dispassionate — with or without vows or fires — may renounce; eligibility is having found desires like vomit.
arguments: Jābāla 4
Maitreya 2.18–20

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the restrictive lists govern ritual renunciation, the open statements define the renouncer by inner dispassion; whether one limits the other is not settled here.

candidate_readings.reading: P4-stage / P1-level: rules for ritual (krama) renunciation vs the knower's inner renunciation open to anyone dispassionate
The Nāradaparivrājaka's own clause that the ineligible who have renounced are still fit for the great saying

question: Is a whole (avayavin) something real over and above its parts?

sides.position: Yes: the whole is a new substance inhering in its parts, perceived as one; otherwise nothing could be perceived (atoms being imperceptible) and a thing could not be held or pulled as one.
arguments: Perception of wholes; the imperceptibility of atoms; holding and pulling (NS 2.1.31–37).
Objections that a whole can reside in its parts neither wholly nor partly are answered (NS 4.2.4–17).

sides.position: No: only the parts (ultimately momentary particulars) are real; the 'whole' is a conceptual construction over an aggregate.
arguments: A whole can occur in its parts neither wholly nor partially (cf. the pūrvapakṣa of NS 4.2.7–10).
What is analysed away by the intellect is not ultimately real (cf. NS 4.2.26).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: the Jain distinction of a standpoint of the enduring whole (dravyārthika) from one of parts and modes (paryāyārthika) would treat the two as partial views.
P1-level: Buddhist two-truth doctrine allows wholes conventional (not ultimate) reality.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Nyāya denies that the whole is merely a standpoint or conventional; the Buddhist logicians deny its reality. Neither accepts the P2 reading.

question: May (or should) a widow follow her husband onto the pyre?

sides.position: The widow's dharma is lifelong chastity and restraint (MDh 5.156–160); Medhātithi (on Manu) holds that following the husband in death is self-destruction, not dharma, comparable to a rite performed to harm.
arguments: the prohibition of taking one's own life
Manu's silence on the practice

sides.position: It is permitted as an option: chastity or ascending the pyre (Viṣṇusmṛti 25.14); the Mitākṣarā (on YS 1.86) defends it as a meritorious optional act.
arguments: an explicit smṛti option
the promised reward

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled.
candidate_readings: Medhātithi's Mīmāṃsā argument that a rite motivated by desire and involving killing is not dharma
the Mitākṣarā's reading as an optional (kāmya) act
later kalivarjya-style prohibitions and the Śākta tantras' prohibition (outside this unit)

question: Can women, and people of every birth (varṇa, jāti), attain liberation — and are they eligible for the scriptures, initiation and renunciation that lead to it?

sides.position: The orthodox order: four classes with distinct duties; the śūdra is not twice-born and may not hear, study or perform the Veda — severe penalties are laid down for one who listens to it; a woman is guarded by father, husband and sons and is not independent; eligibility for the Vedic rite belongs to the twice-born, husband and wife performing jointly. The Veda is not within hearing of women and śūdras — hence the Bhārata was composed for them.

Śūdras are not eligible for the knowledge that comes through Vedic study (BS 1.3.34-38); but Śaṅkara grants that those like Vidura and Dharmavyādha attained knowledge through the impressions of former lives, that the fruit of knowledge once attained cannot be withheld, and that all four classes may hear the Itihāsa and Purāṇa. In the Manīṣāpañcaka, whoever has realized the one consciousness is the teacher, be he caṇḍāla or brāhmaṇa.
Maitreyī was a discusser of Brahman; Satyakāma, who did not know his father, was accepted as a brāhmaṇa for his truthfulness; Jānaśruti, addressed as 'śūdra', was taught by Raikva.

Women cannot attain liberation in a female body: they cannot give up clothing and so cannot be without possessions; they lack the strongest bodily constitution needed for the highest pure meditation; as they cannot fall to the lowest hell they cannot rise to the highest state; the scripture's 'female siddhas' means psychological, not physical, sex (Prabhācandra); subtle living beings arise in their bodies (Aṣṭapāhuḍa). The monk's sign is 'like the newborn' — naked.

Women can attain liberation: the nineteenth Tīrthaṅkara, Mallī, was a woman; the liberated include those liberated in a female form (Prajñāpanā's fifteen kinds); nuns keep their robes by monastic law.

Śākaṭāyana: there is liberation for women as for men, since its cause — the three jewels — is present in them; a woman is not a non-soul, not incapable of liberation, not opposed to right faith, not non-human.

Women who go forth are capable of the fruits up to arahantship (the Buddha to Ānanda), though it is impossible that a woman be a fully awakened Buddha; Mahāpajāpatī's ordination came with eight principles of respect. Somā: what does womanhood matter when the mind is concentrated? Class is not by birth: among humans there is no difference of species; one is a brāhmaṇa by deeds.

The nāga king's eight-year-old daughter attains buddhahood (the Lotus Sūtra, in which she turns into a man); the goddess in Vimalakīrti's house shows Śāriputra that 'woman' has no fixed mark; Amitābha's thirty-fifth vow; in Zen Dōgen urges bowing to anyone who has attained the Way, man or woman.
The Gītā: those who take refuge in me, even of sinful birth — women, vaiśyas and śūdras — reach the highest goal; the learned see the same in a brāhmaṇa, a cow, an elephant, a dog and a dog-eater.

Devotion knows no distinction of caste, learning, beauty, family or wealth; those of every birth down to the lowest are qualified for it; a dog-cooker who has offered all to the Lord is better than a learned brāhmaṇa without devotion; Rāma tells Śabarī that neither sex, caste, name nor stage of life is the cause of worship.
The Lord's devotees, even the lowest of the low below the four castes, are to be honoured as he is; the pāṇar Tiruppāṇ Āḻvār was carried into Śrīraṅgam (the tradition's account).

Wherever devotion to Śiva is strong, low or high, that one is a devotee; among those joined in the one contemplation of Śiva there is no brāhmaṇa or outcaste. Dāsimayya: they call it woman if they see breasts and long hair, man if beard and whiskers — but the self in between is neither.

No one is low by birth; the mud of low deeds makes one low (Ravidās); do not ask a sādhu's caste — ask his knowledge (Kabīr). (The same Kabīr corpus also contains sayings warning against women as a snare — recorded, not harmonised.)

What makes a woman a Paṟaicci or a brāhmaṇī — is there any difference in flesh, skin or bone? (Civavākkiyar); learning, caste distinctions and ritual observances are to be burnt away (Pāmpāṭṭi); mankind is one family and God is one (Tirumantiram).
When the Bhairavī circle has begun, all castes are twice-born; when it is over they are separate again; no caste distinction is to be made in the consecrated food of the supreme Self.

The Kiraṇa, asked whether initiation should follow the ranking of the classes: for women and others incapable of the observances, the guru purifies the observances away and their liberation is through the yoga of devotion in the Śaiva scripture; for the capable the observances remain and knowledge is revealed to them.
Young, old or very old, sick or weak — whoever is diligent attains success in yoga through practice; women and śūdras too may practise breath-control, with a non-Vedic mantra (Yoga-Yājñavalkya).

historical_debates.accounts: Periya Purāṇam (the tradition's account)
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Tamil Śaiva: the outcaste devotee entered Śiva's presence after passing through fire.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the orthodox Vedic order restricts eligibility for Vedic study and rite by birth and sex, the Digambaras deny liberation in a female body, while the Śvetāmbaras and Yāpanīyas, the Buddhists, the bhakti, Vīraśaiva, Sant and Siddha voices and the Kaula tantras open liberation (and in varying degrees initiation) to all.
reconciliation.detail: A distinction used within the orthodox tradition itself narrows the dispute: eligibility (adhikāra) for Vedic study is one thing, liberation another — Śaṅkara (BSBh 1.3.38) grants liberation through smṛti, Purāṇa and former-life impressions, and the Manīṣāpañcaka makes realization, not birth, the mark of the teacher. The critics reject birth-based adhikāra itself. Early Buddhism affirms women's arahantship but denies a female sammāsambuddha.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Digambaras insist on nudity as a condition of liberation and deny it to women (Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa); the Śvetāmbaras and Yāpanīyas reject that argument (Strīnirvāṇaprakaraṇa); Dharmaśāstra and Mīmāṃsā hold the varṇa restrictions to be Vedic; the Sants, Vīraśaivas and Siddhas deny that birth confers any spiritual rank.

candidate_readings: P4-stage (adhikāra): eligibility for particular disciplines (Vedic study, the naked vow) differs by birth or body while liberation itself does not — the orthodox and Digambara form; rejected by the bhakti, Sant, Vīraśaiva and Siddha critics as a restatement of birth-rank, and by the Digambaras as to liberation itself.

P2-standpoint: from the standpoint of the self (neither male nor female — Dāsimayya; the Advaita witness) no distinction; from the standpoint of the body and social order, distinctions — each side accepts only its own half.

P3-path: devotion open to all (NBS 72; BhG 9.32) as a distinct path from Vedic knowledge — accepted by many Vedāntins (Rāmānuja on 9.32) while retaining Vedic restrictions; rejected by the Sants as insufficient.

question: Can a woman, in a woman's body, attain buddhahood?

sides.position: Womanhood is empty like all dharmas: dharmas are neither male nor female (the goddess in Vimalakīrti); Queen Śrīmālā teaches the one vehicle and is predicted to buddhahood; the goddess of the Ganges is predicted; the nāga princess attains buddhahood in an instant.
arguments: Vimalakīrti 6.14-16.
Śrīmālā ch. 1.
Aṣṭasāhasrikā ch. 19.
Lotus ch. 12.

sides.position: A woman's body cannot be a buddha: Śāriputra objects so in the Lotus, and the nāga princess becomes male before appearing as a buddha; Amitābha's and Bhaiṣajyaguru's vows promise women release from the woman's state; the Pali Bahudhātuka Sutta (MN 115) says a woman cannot be a fully awakened buddha.
arguments: Lotus 12 (Śāriputra's objection; the transformation).
Bhaiṣajyaguru's vows.

reconciliation.explanation: The Vimalakīrti itself places the question on two levels: ultimately dharmas are neither male nor female; conventionally bodies and their karmic conditions are spoken of.
reconciliation.detail: Under P1 the goddess's teaching (ultimate) and the sex-change narratives and vows (conventional) do not exclude each other; whether the conventional condition binds final buddhahood is not settled by P1.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Traditions that hold the thirty-two marks (including the male mark) to be required of a buddha keep the conventional restriction as binding.

question: Is liberation won by ritual works, by knowledge alone, by knowledge combined with works, by devotion, or by the Lord's grace — and does grace wait on the soul's surrender (the 'monkey') or carry it without cause (the 'cat')?

sides.position: Dharma, known only from the Veda, yields its fruit; liberation is not enjoined as a fruit of ritual knowledge. For one who knows the self, when earlier actions are exhausted by experience and no new ones arise — by avoiding desire-prompted and forbidden acts and performing the obligatory ones — there is no further embodiment (Kumārila). The self is subsidiary to the rite as its agent (the prior view in BS 3.4.2).

One troubled by the sorrows of transmigration, not longing even for the pleasures mixed with them, turns from prohibited and desire-prompted acts, exhausts the merit and demerit already produced by experiencing them, and by self-knowledge supported by calm, restraint and the like destroys the store of karma and is released.

Knowledge alone liberates: liberation is not something produced, reached, modified or purified by action but the eternal nature of the self; knowledge of an existing thing depends on the thing, not on the person's will; action is not opposed to ignorance and cannot remove it. Works done without desire purify the mind and produce the desire to know (sacrifice, gifts and austerity, BĀU 4.4.22) and are then renounced; knowledge cannot be combined with works, since works require the notions of agent, act and fruit that knowledge removes.

Bhāskara (and before him Bhartṛprapañca): knowledge must be combined with the lifelong performance of prescribed works (jñāna-karma-samuccaya); 'then' in 'then the inquiry into Brahman' means after the inquiry into ritual; release does not come while the body lasts.

Liberating knowledge is not the understanding of a sentence but meditation — continuous, loving remembrance (bhakti) — to which works and knowledge are ancillary; the inquiry into Brahman follows the inquiry into ritual. Or, for those unable, the Lord's own words 'abandoning all dharmas, take refuge in me alone' teach surrender (prapatti).

Vedānta Deśika: surrender (prapatti) is an independent means the soul performs once, with its limbs, and is the occasion of the Lord's grace — as the young monkey clings to its mother (the 'monkey' analogy, markaṭa-nyāya).

Piḷḷai Lokācārya: the Lord alone is the means; surrender is not a means but the acceptance befitting the soul's dependence; his grace is without cause — as the mother cat carries the kitten (the 'cat' analogy, mārjāra-nyāya).
sides.notes: The cat/monkey labels are the traditions' own mnemonic summaries of the difference; the texts argue it in terms of upāya.

sides.position: Without Nārāyaṇa's grace there is no liberation, and without knowledge no abundant grace: grace won by ritual action is the lowest, by hearing and reflection middling, by direct vision the highest; liberation is won by his pleasure alone, with love preceded by knowledge of his greatness.

Devotion is greater than action, knowledge and yoga, being of the nature of the fruit; neither yoga, Sāṃkhya, dharma, study, austerity nor renunciation wins the Lord as strong devotion does; devotion is not an act, since like knowledge it does not depend on effort.

The Gītā: a twofold commitment was declared of old — the yoga of knowledge for the Sāṃkhyas, the yoga of action for the yogins; renunciation and the yoga of action both bring the highest good; Janaka reached perfection by action; the sacrifice of knowledge is better than material sacrifice; not by the Vedas, austerity, gifts or sacrifice but by exclusive devotion can the Lord be seen; performing all actions, taking refuge in him, one attains by his grace; 'abandoning all dharmas, take refuge in me alone'.

The Upaniṣads cited by every side: the self is not attained by instruction, intellect or much learning but by the one whom it chooses; sacrifices are unsafe boats; those who worship ignorance (ritual) enter darkness, and greater darkness those delighting in knowledge alone — by both one crosses death; brāhmaṇas seek to know the self by Veda-study, sacrifice, gifts and austerity.

Ignorance — not mere absence of knowledge but incomplete manifestation — is the cause of transmigration and knowledge the sole cause of liberation; the descent of power (śaktipāta) depends on the Lord's freedom alone, not on a balance of karma, and is intense, middling or mild; initiation leading to nirvāṇa happens for the one who knows this, without oblation.

Bondage by āṇava-mala is a real substance that knowledge alone cannot remove; when the two deeds are balanced and mala has ripened, grace descends and the guru, as Śiva, removes the bonds in initiation — the rite liberates by Śiva's power.

Right view, right knowledge and right conduct together are the path to liberation; knowledge without action is lost and the action of the ignorant is lost. No creator's grace is admitted: the soul frees itself.

In an age without a buddha one cannot reach non-retrogression by self-power; birth in the Pure Land is by the power of Amitābha's vow (other-power); Shinran: even the good are born there, how much more the evil — shinjin and the nembutsu are themselves given.

historical_debates.name: Śaṅkara and Maṇḍana Miśra at Māhiṣmatī
historical_debates.accounts: Śaṅkaradigvijaya 8–10 (the tradition's account): the debate on knowledge versus Vedic ritual, judged by Maṇḍana's wife Ubhaya Bhāratī, who placed a garland on each; Maṇḍana's garland withered first.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Advaita tradition: Maṇḍana accepted that knowledge alone liberates, took renunciation, and became Sureśvara.
historical_debates.scholarly: The identity of Maṇḍana Miśra with Sureśvara is disputed (scholarly account, labelled); Maṇḍana's own Brahmasiddhi holds works helpful to knowledge (see dsp:jnana-karma-samuccaya).

historical_debates.name: The division of the Vaṭakalai and Teṅkalai
historical_debates.accounts: Vedānta Deśika's Rahasyatrayasāra; Piḷḷai Lokācārya's Śrīvacana Bhūṣaṇam and Mumukṣuppaḍi with Maṇavāḷa Māmuni's commentaries; the traditions list eighteen differences (see dsp:vadakalai-tenkalai).
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Both traditions continue; each holds its account of prapatti and grace to be Rāmānuja's.

historical_debates.name: Hōnen at Ōhara
historical_debates.accounts: Hōnen Shōnin Gyōjō Ezu: before Tendai and Nara scholars Hōnen explained birth by the nembutsu of the vow for ordinary beings of this age.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Jōdo tradition: the scholars were persuaded.

reconciliation.explanation: Reconciled in part by the texts' own ordering: works purify the mind and produce the desire to know (P4-stage — Advaita, Bhāmatī), the Gītā's two commitments for two kinds of people and the Uddhava Gītā's three yogas for different temperaments (P3-path); whether knowledge alone or knowledge with works finally liberates, whether devotion is a means or the goal beyond liberation, and whether grace takes the soul's surrender as its condition remain not yet reconciled.
reconciliation.detail: P4: BSBh 3.4.26 and the Bhāmatī make works a preliminary to knowledge; Rāmānuja makes karma- and jñāna-yoga ancillary to bhakti; Madhva grades grace by the means that wins it. P3: BhG 3.3 ('a twofold commitment'), Uddhava Gītā 11.20.6-8 ('knowledge, action and devotion — there is no other'). What is not reconciled: samuccaya (Bhāskara) vs knowledge alone (Śaṅkara); Mīmāṃsā's liberation by exhausting karma vs Vedānta's knowledge; prapatti as a means (Vaṭakalai) vs no means (Teṅkalai); self-power vs other-power; grace by the Lord's freedom (Trika) vs grace occasioned by ripened mala (Siddhānta).
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Śaṅkara rejects samuccaya (Gītā-bhāṣya intro to 2.11; BĀU-bhāṣya 5.1.1); Bhāskara rejects knowledge alone; the bhakti schools deny that devotion is merely preparatory (NBS 25-26); the Teṅkalai deny that surrender is a means, the Vaṭakalai affirm it; Jōdo Shinshū denies any self-power; the Jains admit no grace.

candidate_readings: P8-six-marks: the Gītā's purport by opening and close — knowledge (Śaṅkara, from 2.11 and 18.66 as renunciation), devotion (Rāmānuja, Madhusūdana's closing verse), action (recent readings) — see dsp:gita-primary-teaching.

P7-arthavada: praise of works, of knowledge or of devotion as 'greater than all others' read as praise rather than exclusive doctrine — each school reads the others' texts so and rejects that reading of its own.
P1-level: works valid at the empirical level, knowledge alone at the ultimate — Advaita's own form, rejected by Bhāskara and by the bhakti schools.

cat and monkey (P2-standpoint): from the Lord's side grace is causeless, from the soul's side surrender is its fitting response — offered within Śrīvaiṣṇavism but not accepted as dissolving the eighteen differences.

question: Is this world a 'frame of illusion' to be seen through, or a 'mansion of mirth' to be enjoyed in the Lord?

sides.position: (Rāmprasād) 'This world is a frame of illusion' — the mind should not be deceived by it but turn to the Mother.
(Āju Gosāi, a Vaiṣṇava contemporary, in the tradition's account) 'This world is a mansion of mirth' (majār kuṭi), where one eats, drinks and makes merry with the Lord.

historical_debates.name: Rāmprasād and Āju Gosāi's song-exchange
historical_debates.accounts: Bengali oral tradition; later cited by Ramakrishna (U52).
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Remembered as a friendly contest of songs.

reconciliation.explanation: The same world is a trap to the one still bound and a mansion of mirth to the one who has realised the Lord (Mother) in it — the reading given in the Ramakrishna tradition.
reconciliation.detail: Recorded as the later tradition's reconciliation (U52 to anchor in the Kathāmṛta); both songs are quoted there.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: None recorded; the exchange is remembered as good-humoured.

question: Is the world real, or an appearance (mithyā) that is neither real nor unreal, superimposed on the one reality — and is māyā an indeterminable ignorance or the Lord's real power?

sides.position: The world is mithyā: not real, since it is sublated by the knowledge of Brahman; not unreal, since it appears; indeterminable as either — like the silver seen in shell. Duality is mere māyā; non-duality is the ultimate truth. Three orders are distinguished: the ultimate (Brahman), the empirical (the world, real for all practical purposes — Śaṅkara defends external objects against the Buddhist idealist), and the illusory (dream, rope-snake). Falsity is defended under five definitions against the Dvaita critique.

The world of souls and matter is real, the body of Brahman. The Advaitin's avidyā is untenable in seven ways — no locus, no power to conceal self-luminous Brahman, no coherent nature, no sense to 'indescribable', no means of knowledge, no remover, no removal; no means of knowledge establishes an undifferentiated reality; consciousness is always someone's and of something.

The world is real: the witness (sākṣin) establishes it as unsublated; what is sublated produces no effect; even dream-objects are real products of impressions. None of the five Advaita definitions of falsity is coherent, and the inferences from 'perceivable', 'insentient' and 'limited' fail. Reality is twofold: the independent (Viṣṇu) and the dependent (souls and matter) — dependent, but real.
The effect is real and both different and non-different from its cause; those who expound māyā lead people astray (Bhāskara).

The world is a real transformation of the Lord's external power; the souls are his marginal power, distinct yet dependent. To call the world false and the Lord's lordship imagined is the māyāvāda that the Gītā (16.8) describes and the Padma Purāṇa calls 'Buddhism in disguise'.

The universe is the real self-manifestation of free consciousness on its own screen; māyā is the Lord's power of self-concealment (Māyā-śakti), his supreme freedom — not an indeterminable ignorance. Those who say 'in the beginning this was being' stand at the level of the Īśvara-tattva, and some knowers of the Upaniṣads take prāṇa as the self: partial roles of the one consciousness. (The Vijñāna Bhairava nevertheless teaches contemplating the universe as a magic show as one means to peace.)
Māyā is the Goddess's own power; she is the manifest and the unmanifest; her reality is beyond both duality and non-duality (see dsp:maya-sakti-or-avidya).

The world is real, produced from real māyā by Śiva as efficient cause; 'advaita' in the Śivajñānabodha means non-separateness, not numerical identity; the Advaita and other views are set out and refuted.
The world is real, being produced by faultless causes and never sublated; bondage cannot be due to an unreal avidyā — and a real avidyā would abandon non-dualism.
Absolute non-duality is refuted: if all were one there would be no distinction of act and fruit, merit and demerit, this world and the next, knowledge and ignorance, bondage and release.
The idealist and illusionist thesis lacks a reason: the notion of dream-objects depends on prior waking experience, as memory does; false cognition presupposes a real object mistaken.

All dharmas, the fruits of the path and buddhahood itself are like an illusion, like a dream — appearing conventionally, empty of own-nature; form is emptiness and emptiness form (the Prajñāpāramitā background shared by the Mahāyāna schools).

historical_debates.name: The Nyāyāmṛta–Advaitasiddhi exchange
historical_debates.accounts: Vyāsatīrtha's Nyāyāmṛta attacks the Advaita definitions of falsity and the inferences for it; Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's Advaitasiddhi answers it section by section; Vyāsa Rāmācārya's Nyāyāmṛta-taraṅgiṇī defends the Nyāyāmṛta; Brahmānanda Sarasvatī's Laghucandrikā (Gauḍabrahmānandī) defends the Advaitasiddhi; later rejoinders continued (e.g. the Nyāyāmṛta-kaṇṭakoddhāra and the Nyāyāmṛta-āmoda in the Dvaita line).
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Each tradition holds that its own side prevailed; neither presents the exchange as closed.
historical_debates.notes: The order of the later rejoinders is given from memory (moderate confidence).

historical_debates.name: Rāmānuja and Yajñamūrti at Śrīraṅgam
historical_debates.accounts: Guruparamparāprabhāvam (Ārāyirappaṭi) — the tradition's account
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Śrīvaiṣṇava: after eighteen days the Advaita renouncer Yajñamūrti yielded and became Rāmānuja's disciple.

historical_debates.name: Śaṅkara's debates in the digvijaya narratives
historical_debates.accounts: Śaṅkaradigvijaya (the tradition's account)
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Advaita: Śaṅkara defeated the dualist and ritualist schools of his time.
historical_debates.notes: Named opponents and places vary between the digvijaya texts; see also dsp:works-knowledge-grace for Maṇḍana.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: Advaita's own levels of reality make the world real empirically and false ultimately, but Viśiṣṭādvaita, Dvaita, Śaiva Siddhānta and Kashmir Śaivism reject the very distinction as applied to the world, each for its own reasons.
reconciliation.detail: Advaita offers P1 in its own terms (the world is vyāvahārika-sat; BSBh 2.2.28 upholds external objects against the Buddhist idealist). The theistic Vedāntas deny that anything can be empirically real and ultimately false (Śrībhāṣya 1.1.1; Nyāyāmṛta 1). Kashmir Śaivism agrees that the world depends on one consciousness but calls it that consciousness's real self-display and māyā its power, not avidyā — a difference both sides keep.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Rāmānuja's seven untenabilities of avidyā (Śrībhāṣya 1.1.1); Vyāsatīrtha's refutation of the five definitions of falsity (Nyāyāmṛta); Madhva's rejection of vivarta (Anuvyākhyāna 1.4.95-98); the Kashmir Śaiva view of māyā as Śakti (Paramārthasāra 15); Advaita in turn holds that any real second to Brahman conflicts with the non-dual texts (MK 1.17; Advaitasiddhi).

candidate_readings: P1-level (Advaita's own): the world is real at the empirical level and false only from the standpoint of Brahman — rejected by Viśiṣṭādvaita and Dvaita, for whom whatever is, is real, and the empirical/ultimate distinction is not scriptural.

P2-standpoint: from the side of the one consciousness there is no second, from the side of the embodied soul the world is real — rejected by Madhva and Rāmānuja, who hold the world real from every standpoint, and by Advaita if it implies that the world's reality is ultimate.

P4-stage: Kṣemarāja ranks the Vedāntins' 'being' at the Īśvara-tattva, and the Vijñāna Bhairava prescribes seeing the world as a magic show as a practice (VBT 102, 133) — a practice-level use of the 'appearance' view that does not settle its truth.
vivarta vs ābhāsa (Advaita vs Kashmir Śaivism): both deny that the one consciousness changes; they differ whether its appearing is real self-display or indeterminable — kept apart by both.

question: Did Pātañjala Yoga take its shared meditative and ethical vocabulary (the four attitudes, the five faculties, the afflictions, samāpatti, dharmamegha) from Buddhism, or do Yoga, Buddhism and Jainism draw on a common śramaṇa milieu?

sides.position: Yoga is an ancient teaching (the tradition names Hiraṇyagarbha as its first teacher and Patañjali as its compiler); the Yoga text marks its difference from the Buddhists, rejecting the view that objects are constructions of a single mind; no dependence on Buddhism is acknowledged.
arguments: one object is shared by many minds and does not depend on a single mind (YS 4.15–16)
the bhāṣya states and refutes the idealist argument (YBh 4.14)

sides.position: The suttas themselves acknowledge that other wanderers taught the abandoning of the hindrances and the four immeasurables, and that the bodhisatta learned the formless attainments from other teachers; the Buddha's distinctiveness lies in knowing where these culminate and in the liberating insight beyond them.
arguments: 'we too teach our disciples thus' (SN 46.54)
each liberation of mind has a stated culmination only the Tathāgata can explain (SN 46.54)
the formless attainments learned from Āḷāra and Uddaka were judged insufficient (MN 26)

sides.position: The five great vows and the four reflections belong to the Jina's teaching; Haribhadra treats the yoga taught by others as one path of qualities under different names, correlating his eight views with the limbs beginning with yama.
arguments: the five vows and the name mahāvrata (TS 7.1–2)
the four reflections toward classes of beings (TS 7.11)
the eight views correlated with the eight limbs (YDS 16)

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: a historical question on which the traditions' own accounts and the scholarly hypotheses differ; no principle settles history.
candidate_readings: Common milieu: the object-class form of the four attitudes (YS 1.33 = TS 7.11, unlike the Pali formula) and the shared five vows suggest a common śramaṇa stock rather than one-way borrowing.
Specific borrowing: technical terms of Buddhist Abhidharma (anuśaya, the burnt seed, dharmamegha as a ground-name) may have been taken over by the Yoga authors (scholarly hypothesis).
P2-standpoint (doctrinal content only): the same practices described from different standpoints — boundless pervasion (Buddhist) versus attitudes suited to classes of beings (Yoga, Jain).
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Yoga tradition does not acknowledge dependence on Buddhism; the Buddhist tradition claims its path differs in culmination; the Jain tradition derives its vows from the Jinas.

notes: Borrowing evidence: brw:buddhism-yoga-four-attitudes, brw:buddhism-yoga-five-faculties, brw:buddhism-yoga-klesa-theory, brw:buddhism-yoga-meditation-vocabulary, brw:mahayana-yoga-dharmamegha, brw:jain-four-bhavanas-and-yoga, brw:jain-mahavratas-and-yoga-yamas, brw:four-immeasurables-sramana-common, brw:yoga-refutes-buddhist-idealism.

question: What place, if any, has yogic discipline (haṭha, aṣṭāṅga, kuṇḍalinī) on the Sant path of the Name?

sides.position: None as a means: sahaj is best — no closing of eyes, stopping of ears or mortification; the yogī dyes his clothes, not his mind; the Name and love suffice.
arguments: forced yoga breeds pride and display
the Lord is found by love and the Name

sides.position: Sundardās teaches aṣṭāṅga and haṭha yoga (postures, breath, cakras, the serpent power) as a stage within the Sant path, below devotion and knowledge.
Caraṇdās teaches the eight limbs of yoga to his disciples as a support of devotion to Kṛṣṇa and the guru.
Only the yoga of the sound current, beginning at the eye centre, is needed; haṭha and kuṇḍalinī work on the lower centres is unnecessary and hazardous; surat-śabd yoga is the crown of yogas.

reconciliation.explanation: Sundardās and Caraṇdās themselves place yoga as a preparatory stage (P4) under the Name and devotion; temperaments differ (P3).
reconciliation.detail: Claims only that the Sant tradition contains this graded view; it does not claim that Kabīr's verses or Sant Mat accept yoga as a stage.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Kabīr's verses reject forced yoga outright; Sant Mat rejects lower-centre yoga as unnecessary; for the Nāth side of the wider question see dsp:kabir-and-the-yogis (U21).

notes: Intra-Sant counterpart of dsp:kabir-and-the-yogis (U21, Nāth vs Sant), which records the Kabīr–Gorakh goṣṭhī.

question: Is knowledge alone sufficient for liberation, or must bodily yoga accompany it?

sides.position: Yoga and knowledge together: knowledge without yoga cannot liberate, and the mere knower is reborn until his body is 'ripened' by yoga.
arguments: Yogatattva 14–15

sides.position: Knowledge alone gives kaivalya; bodily yoga is for the unawakened; realization is not samādhi or yogic attainment but oneness with Brahman.
arguments: Muktikā prose: not by works, Sāṃkhya, yoga or worship
Tejobindu 1.33: nose-pressing for the ignorant
Mahāvākya 5

reconciliation.explanation: The Śāṇḍilya names two ways of ending mind — yoga and knowledge — suited to different people, and the Varāha's bird and ant paths both reach Brahman.
reconciliation.detail: Śāṇḍilya 1.41 (P3) and Varāha 4.34–42 (P4) treat yoga and knowledge as routes for different temperaments and stages; the Tejobindu keeps the limbs but reads them as knowledge.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Yogaśikhā explicitly rejects 'knowledge alone'; the Muktikā explicitly excludes yoga as a means of kaivalya.

notes: Related registry dispute: dsp:works-knowledge-grace.

checks.note: The inline refs and paraphrased content were checked against the e-text passages read for the teachings. All 9 teachings it rests on exist and were located in the e-text. Some rest on teachings whose ref was corrected or only partly confirmed; the content is located, only the numbering changes: tea:mahavakya-upanisad:5 (corrected).

question: Is Īśvara to be admitted, and is devotion to him a means to liberation? (Yoga against nirīśvara Sāṃkhya)

sides.position: Īśvara is a special puruṣa, ever free, unsurpassed in knowledge, the teacher of the ancients, designated by Oṃ; devotion to him brings samādhi near.
arguments: The seed of omniscience admits degrees, so it has a limit where it is unsurpassed (YBh 1.25).
Two equal lords could not both have their contrary wishes fulfilled, so lordship without equal exists (YBh 1.24).
Won over by devotion, Īśvara favours the yogin by mere intention (YBh 1.23).

Vijñānabhikṣu: Sāṃkhya teaches liberation from knowledge of the self alone; Yoga shows knowledge of the Supreme Lord as the swift cause of liberation (YV 1.51), and Sāṃkhya is contained in Yoga as rivers in the ocean (YV intro.).

sides.position: Liberation comes from discriminating knowledge of puruṣa and prakṛti; Īśvara is not established by any means of knowledge and is not needed to explain the working of prakṛti.
arguments: Prakṛti acts for the puruṣa's purpose unconsciously, as milk flows for the calf (Sāṃkhya Kārikā 57).
'Because Īśvara is not established' (Sāṃkhya Sūtra 1.92).
sides.note: Stated from memory in Sāṃkhya's own terms; U09 owns the Sāṃkhya texts.

historical_debates.name: The Sāṃkhya–Yoga contest reported by Bhīṣma
historical_debates.accounts: Mahābhārata 12 (Mokṣadharma; c. ch. 289 CE): the Yogins argue 'how can one without a Lord be liberated?', the Sāṃkhyas praise knowledge; both are declared valid. Recalled from memory, reference to be checked.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Both views accepted as leading to the highest goal.

reconciliation.explanation: The Gītā (5.4–5) and the Mokṣadharma treat Sāṃkhya and Yoga as two approaches to one goal (P3), and Vijñānabhikṣu reads the Sāṃkhya denial of Īśvara as a provisional, concessive argument (P5).
reconciliation.detail: What is reconciled is the soteriological convergence (both end in discriminative knowledge and kaivalya); the ontological question whether a special puruṣa exists is not settled by P3.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Nirīśvara Sāṃkhya authors argue on their own terms that Īśvara is unproven, not merely provisionally set aside; Vijñānabhikṣu's reading is a Yoga-Vedānta commentator's view.

notes: Narrower recorded debate within dsp:isvara (owned by U50).

question: Is cognition (the dependent nature) real, or is it empty of own-being like everything else? — Yogācāra and Madhyamaka

sides.position: The dependent nature — unreal imagination — exists; only the duality it projects is absent; emptiness is the absence of that duality and itself exists. Taken literally, 'all dharmas lack own-nature' is a provisional teaching (second turning); its intended meaning is the three naturelessnesses. To deny the dependent and the perfected as well is the worst nihilism.
arguments: If nothing existed, there would be neither defilement nor purification, and effort would be fruitless (MAV 1.22).
Emptiness must be the emptiness of something: of duality in unreal imagination (MAV 1.2, 1.14).
The Bodhisattvabhūmi (tattvārtha chapter) condemns those who deny the inexpressible reality as nihilists (recalled).

sides.position: Cognition is as empty of own-being as its objects; if the dependent existed by own-being it could not originate dependently. The ālaya and cognition-only were taught provisionally for those who fear emptiness; reflexive awareness is incoherent, as a sword cannot cut itself.
arguments: Bhāviveka criticizes Yogācāra in the Madhyamakahṛdaya (ch. 5) and Prajñāpradīpa (recalled).
Candrakīrti's Madhyamakāvatāra ch. 6 refutes cognition-only, the ālaya as ultimately real and reflexive awareness.
Śāntideva (Bodhicaryāvatāra ch. 9) refutes reflexive awareness with the lamp and sword examples.

sides.position: Mind-only is correct conventionally and is the step by which external objects are negated; ultimately mind too is neither one nor many and so without own-being; the Laṅkāvatāra's verses show the sequence.
arguments: Śāntarakṣita, Madhyamakālaṃkāra (vv. 91–93, recalled): riding the chariot of the two systems.
Kamalaśīla reads Laṅkāvatāra 10.256–258 as stages of meditation.

sides.position: Image-free luminous awareness is the ultimate meaning of both Yogācāra and Madhyamaka; the images alone are false.
arguments: Ratnākaraśānti presents his view as the Madhyamaka of the Prajñāpāramitā (recalled).

historical_debates.name: Bhāviveka and Dharmapāla
historical_debates.accounts: Xuanzang's record: Bhāviveka travelled to debate Dharmapāla, who declined; Bhāviveka then retired to a cave to await Maitreya's coming (recalled).
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: no debate held

historical_debates.name: Candrakīrti and Candragomin at Nālandā
historical_debates.accounts: Tibetan histories: a debate of many years, Candragomin (for Yogācāra) consulting Avalokiteśvara at night.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Tibetan accounts praise both; no decisive victory recorded

reconciliation.explanation: P4/P1: the Laṅkāvatāra's own four-stage sequence and Yogācāra-Madhyamaka treat mind-only as a stage and a conventional truth on the way to the imageless; this reconciles the two as successive levels for those who accept that sequence.
reconciliation.detail: The reconciliation is itself a school position (Śāntarakṣita, Kamalaśīla), not a neutral one.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Classical Yogācāra (Asaṅga, Vasubandhu, Sthiramati, Dharmapāla) holds the third turning, not the second, to be definitive and would reject being ranked as a lower stage; Prāsaṅgika (Candrakīrti) rejects even the conventional status of cognition-only and reflexive awareness as taught by Yogācāra.

notes: Should be linked with U40's Madhyamaka disputes and dsp:which-turning-is-definitive (U39).

question: Are the four quarters of the yuga equal, or in the proportion 4:3:2:1?

sides.position: Āryabhaṭa: the four quarters of the yuga are equal; the kalpa has 14 Manus of 72 yugas; the yuga has an ascending and a descending half.
arguments: computational uniformity of the revolutions

sides.position: Brahmagupta and the Sūrya Siddhānta: Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara and Kali are four, three, two and one tenths of the yuga, following the feet of dharma; 'not one of Āryabhaṭa's quarters agrees with the smṛti'.
arguments: the smṛti's authority
the decline of dharma by quarters

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: Āryabhaṭa's equal quarters serve computation (gaṇita) while the 4:3:2:1 scheme expresses the decline of dharma (smṛti) — but Brahmagupta explicitly rejects this separation.
Brahmagupta's reading: Āryabhaṭa simply erred against scripture.
Recent: Sri Yukteswar's 24,000-year cycle (The Holy Science, 1894) departs from both (recent: true).
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Brahmagupta treats agreement with smṛti as binding on astronomy; Āryabhaṭa's followers kept his system.

historical_debates.name: Brahmagupta's critique of Āryabhaṭa
historical_debates.accounts: Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta 1.9 and ch. 11 (tantraparīkṣā)
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: The Brāhma and Saura schools follow the 4:3:2:1 scheme; the Āryapakṣa kept Āryabhaṭa's constants.
